differentiation.extension: Give the pair a third charge q3 at a different position on the same line. Ask them to compute the net electrostatic force on q1 from q2 and q3 by calculating both forces with units, assigning directions (signs), and adding them vectorially to produce a single net force magnitude and direction in newtons. Explain how superposition leads to the net force.
differentiation.support: If you are stuck, use this sentence frame and worked first item. Frame: 'F is proportional to |q1 q2| and inversely proportional to r^2, so F = k·|q1 q2|/r^2. Substituting k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2, q1 = __ C, q2 = __ C, r = __ m gives F = 8.99×10^9 × (|q1 q2|) / r^2 = __ N.' Worked example: If q1 = +2.0×10^-6 C, q2 = -3.0×10^-6 C, r = 0.20 m then |q1 q2| = 6.0×10^-12 C^2, r^2 = 0.040 m^2, so F = 8.99×10^9 × 6.0×10^-12 / 0.040 = 1.35 N toward q2 (because charges are opposite). Pair lower-reading students with a stronger reader for calculation checking.

materials: One printed slip per pair with values for q1, q2 (in coulombs) and separation r (in metres)
Whiteboard or chart paper and marker (teacher)
student_instructions: 1. Read the slip your teacher gave your pair. Record q1 (in C), q2 (in C), and r (in m).

2. Derive the form of Coulomb's law step by step on your scrap paper: say F ∝ |q1 q2|, then F ∝ 1/r^2, combine to write F = k·|q1 q2|/r^2. Label k with units: k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2. Show units: C·C gives C^2; r^2 gives m^2; k cancels m^2/C^2 to give N.
3. Substitute the numerical values from your slip into F = k·|q1 q2|/r^2. Compute the magnitude using your calculator and write the answer with units N to two significant figures (or as appropriate).

4. Determine direction: draw two charges on your paper, write their signs, then state whether the force on q1 is toward q2 (attraction) or away from q2 (repulsion). Write the force as a vector statement such as 'F_on_q1 = 3.4 × 10^-3 N toward q2 along the line joining them.'
5. If either q is zero or very small, note that the force will be zero or very small and record that with units. Prepare one sentence with your final magnitude, units, and direction to report.
success_criteria: Each pair writes the algebraic form F = k·|q1 q2|/r^2 on their paper and labels k with its units N·m^2/C^2.
Each pair shows a numerical substitution with units carried through (C, m) and computes a magnitude in newtons on their calculator.
Each pair has a small sketch of the two charges and can point to whether the force is toward or away from the other charge, with that direction written in words on their paper.
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in pairs. Hand each pair one printed slip containing two point charges q1 and q2 and their separation r. Tell students they have 12 minutes to derive Coulomb's law and calculate the force magnitude and direction for their numbers.

2. At the start say: 'We will derive Coulomb's law from the proportionality idea, then use it to compute a numerical force with units. Use k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2.' Write on the whiteboard the three-step derivation outline: (a) force magnitude is proportional to |q1 q2|, (b) it decreases with the square of the distance → divide by r^2, (c) combine with constant k to give F = k |q1 q2| / r^2 with units N. Underline units of each quantity as you say them: coulomb (C), metre (m), newton (N).

3. While pairs work, circulate. For any pair that substitutes numbers incorrectly, point to the units and ask: 'What are the units of q1·q2 and of r^2? How do they produce newtons when multiplied by k?' If a pair is stuck setting direction, prompt them to draw the two charges on paper and decide attraction versus repulsion depending on sign.

4. After 9 minutes, ask pairs to stop calculations and prepare a one-sentence result on their paper giving the force magnitude in newtons, the direction (toward or away), and a short reason based on charge signs. Collect three volunteers to read results in the final 2-3 minutes and correct any arithmetic or unit mistakes on the board.
activities.title: Compute the Coulomb Force Between Two Point Charges

differentiation.extension: A continuous line of three charges along the x-axis: q1 = +2.0×10^-6 C at x = 0.00 m, q2 = -1.0×10^-6 C at x = 0.05 m, q3 = -1.0×10^-6 C at x = 0.15 m. Calculate the net force on q1 (magnitude and direction). Then explain whether the result would change if the signs of q2 and q3 were both flipped to positive, and why, using superposition and algebraic signs.
differentiation.support: If you are stuck start here: worked first item — Problem 1: net charge = +4.80×10^-19 C. Divide by e = 1.60×10^-19 C: 4.80×10^-19 C ÷ 1.60×10^-19 C = 3. So the object has +3 elementary charges (three excess protons or three missing electrons). Sentence frame for Problem 4: “The extra negative charge is due to extra electrons (particle = electron). Rubbing does not create charge because charge is conserved; the electrons moved from ___ to ___, changing distribution but not the total number of electrons in the isolated system.” If needed, pair a student who is unsure with the stronger reader in the pair.

materials: printed worksheet (one per student) or whiteboard
student_instructions: Work with your partner. Show all steps and include units in every calculation.

Problem 1 (Quantisation): A small isolated object has net charge +4.80×10^-19 C. Assume only electrons and protons carry charge. Determine (a) how many excess protons or missing electrons correspond to this net charge? State the integer number and justify why it must be an integer. (Use e = 1.60×10^-19 C.)

Problem 2 (Coulomb magnitude & direction): Two point charges lie on the x-axis. q1 = +3.2×10^-6 C at x = 0.00 m and q2 = -1.6×10^-6 C at x = 0.10 m. (a) Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force on q2 due to q1. (b) Give the direction of that force as a unit-vector or as ‘left/right’ along the x-axis. Use k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2.

Problem 3 (Superposition): Add a third charge q3 = +3.2×10^-6 C at x = 0.20 m. Calculate the net electrostatic force (magnitude and direction) on q2 from q1 and q3. Show the vector addition step explicitly and include units (N).

Problem 4 (Conservation and microscopic origin): A neutral metal sphere is struck by a charged rod and afterward has net charge -6.4×10^-19 C. Explain in two sentences where that extra negative charge came from (name the particle) and why rubbing does not create charge but redistributes it. Use the idea of conservation of charge and quantisation in your answer.
success_criteria: Each pair writes an integer value for number of electrons/protons in Problem 1 and shows the division: net charge (C) ÷ e (C) = integer.

For Problems 2 and 3 each pair shows numeric substitution into Coulomb’s law with units (N·m^2/C^2, C, m), computes magnitudes, and indicates direction on the x-axis (left or right or using ±x unit vector).
In Problem 3 each pair writes the two pairwise forces on q2 separately, shows their vector sum (with signs), and gives the final magnitude and direction.
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in pairs and hand out the worksheet. Say: “You have 10 minutes to complete 4 short problems about charge quantisation, Coulomb’s law, and superposition. Show all units and steps.” Start a visible 10-minute timer.

2. Read aloud the first problem so every pair hears one worked example: explain that e = 1.60×10^-19 C and that charges must be integer multiples of e. While pairs work, circulate and watch for the two misconceptions listed below. If a pair seems stuck after 3 minutes, give the scaffold in the support box verbatim.
3. At 6 minutes remaining, announce time checks and prompt pairs who finished to attempt the extension. Collect worksheets at the end of 10 minutes.
4. After collection, note any recurring errors (units, vector sign/direction, non-integer charge answers, rubbing-creates-charge statements) to address in the next whole-class debrief.
activities.title: Pairwise Coulomb Forces and Charge Quantisation Problems

differentiation.extension: For students who finish early: place two point charges along a line, Q1 = +4.0×10^-6 C at x = 0.10 m and Q2 = −2.0×10^-6 C at x = 0.30 m. Calculate the net electric field vector at x = 0.20 m along the line. Show vector directions, compute magnitudes from each charge with units, and give the algebraic sum (include sign and final unit N/C).
differentiation.support: If you are unsure how to start, copy and complete this sentence frame: “The electric field at a point is E = F/q0. If a test charge q0 = 1.0×10^-6 C feels a force F = 4.5×10^-3 N away from the source, then E = ____ N/C.” Also, use this worked first item to guide you: k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2; for Q = 5.0×10^-6 C and r = 0.20 m, compute E = kQ/r^2 = (8.99×10^9)(5.0×10^-6)/(0.20^2) = (8.99×10^9×5.0×10^-6)/(0.04) = (44.95×10^3)/0.04 = 1.12×10^6 N/C. Show the units at each multiplication and division step.

materials: one plastic rod (e.g., PVC or acrylic) or plastic ruler
a piece of wool or cloth for rubbing
one lightweight test probe: small crumpled paper ball (~1 cm) with a tiny piece of aluminum foil taped on, tied to a 20–30 cm length of cotton thread
stopwatch or classroom clock (optional for timed steps)
whiteboard or chart paper and marker for teacher derivation
student_instructions: Watch the teacher charge the rod and hold it near the suspended test probe. Note whether the probe moves toward or away from the rod and the approximate distance between rod and probe in metres.

Write the operational definition in this sentence: “The electric field E at a point is the force on a positive test charge q0 placed there divided by q0, so E = F/q0.” Include units: force in N, charge in C, so E in N/C.
Observe the teacher’s algebra: start from Coulomb’s law F = (1/4πε0) Q q0 / r^2 r̂, divide by q0, and copy the result E(r) = (1/4πε0) Q / r^2 r̂. Label each symbol with its SI unit on your paper.

Follow the worked numeric example on the board. Then, using the same numbers, check the direction: if Q is positive, draw an arrow showing the field at the probe location; if Q were negative, draw the arrow pointing the opposite way.

Answer two quick items on your paper: (a) What is the measured direction of the force on the probe in your observation (toward or away from the rod)? (b) What is the magnitude of E for Q = +5.0×10^−6 C at r = 0.20 m (show units and calculation)?
success_criteria: Each pair can point to the charged rod (source charge) and the suspended probe (test charge) and say whether the probe was attracted or repelled.
Each student copy shows the operational definition E = F/q0 with units N/C written next to E.
At least one member of each pair writes the numeric calculation for E using Q = 5.0×10^−6 C and r = 0.20 m, including units at every step and a final magnitude in N/C.
teacher_instructions: Group students into pairs. Place materials at each pair’s table. Say: “We will demonstrate how a source charge produces an electric field, how we define that field operationally, and how to calculate its magnitude and direction for a point charge.”

Demonstration start (0–2 minutes): Rub the plastic rod with the wool to build charge. Hold the rod near (but not touching) the suspended test probe so the probe is free to move. Ask pairs to watch from their seats and note whether the probe is attracted or repelled and in which direction it moves relative to the rod.

Derive the operational definition (2–5 minutes): On the board, write: electric field E at a point = force on a positive test charge q0 placed there divided by q0, E = F/q0. Explain units: force in newtons (N), charge in coulombs (C), so E has units N/C. While you explain, ask one pair to place their probe 0.10 m from the rod and report the direction of the force on the probe (toward or away from the rod).

Derive E for a point source charge (5–8 minutes): Using Coulomb’s law F = (1/4πε0) Q q0 / r^2 r̂, divide both sides by q0 to obtain E(r) = (1/4πε0) Q / r^2 r̂. Point to each symbol, state its SI unit (Q in C, r in m, E in N/C). On the board compute a worked example with numbers: take Q = +5.0×10^−6 C, r = 0.20 m, and compute magnitude E = kQ/r^2 with k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2; carry units through every step.

Class check and wrap-up (8–10 minutes): Ask pairs to compare the observed direction (attraction or repulsion) with the sign of Q in the worked example and state: for positive Q field points away from Q; for negative Q field points toward Q. While pairs discuss, circulate to confirm that each pair can point to the probe and rod and state the direction and estimate the distance used.
activities.title: Probe a Charged Rod with a Suspended Test Charge

differentiation.extension: Replace the uniform field with a non-uniform field that changes with x as E(x) = E₀ + α x (units N·C⁻¹ where x in m). Ask: for small α (units N·C⁻¹·m⁻¹), estimate the net force on the dipole to first order in α, expressing the result in terms of p, α and a. Show units and give a numerical example.
differentiation.support: Sentence frames and worked first item: "Dipole moment p = q × 2a = (____ C) × (____ m) = ____ C·m directed from −q to +q." Worked example: if q = 2.0×10⁻⁶ C and 2a = 0.10 m, then p = (2.0×10⁻⁶ C)(0.10 m) = 2.0×10⁻⁷ C·m. For the midpoint field, compute magnitude of each point-charge field using E = k|q|/r² with r = a (show k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²·C⁻²). Use component addition: E_total,x = E_+x + E_-x, E_total,y = E_+y + E_-y.

materials: One printed 1-page worksheet per pair (teacher can copy in 2 minutes)
student_instructions: 1. Read the setup: two point charges +q and −q are on the x-axis, separated by distance 2a. The midpoint is at the origin. The uniform external electric field is E = (E magnitude) N·C⁻¹ at angle θ above +x. (All numbers are on your worksheet.)
2. Compute the dipole moment p: multiply q (in coulombs, C) by separation 2a (in metres, m). Write p with direction from −q to +q and unit C·m. Show p as an arrow on the diagram.

3. Use the superposition principle to find the electric field at the midpoint: compute the field due to +q and −q separately at the midpoint, write each field as a vector with units N·C⁻¹, then add them componentwise to get E_mid (show arithmetic).

4. Compute electric flux through the small square of side s (given in metres) centered at the midpoint whose normal is +x: use Φ = E · A = E_x · A where A = s² (m²). Show units N·m²·C⁻¹ and state whether flux is positive or negative (based on outward normal).

5. Find the torque on the dipole: draw vectors p and E on the diagram, measure the angle φ between them with the protractor, then compute the torque magnitude |τ| = |p||E| sinφ. Write τ as a vector using right-hand rule (direction of p × E) and give units N·m. Finally, answer: does a net force act on the dipole in this uniform field? Explain in one sentence.
success_criteria: Each pair shows p calculated with correct units C·m on their worksheet and an arrow drawn from −q to +q.
Each pair writes component values for the two fields at the midpoint and shows their vector sum (numbers in N·C⁻¹) using superposition.
Each pair computes a torque magnitude with correct units N·m and states a one-sentence conclusion that net force = 0 in a uniform E.
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in pairs. Distribute one worksheet and a ruler/protractor to each pair. Tell students: “You have 10 minutes to complete the worksheet. Work together and write numbers with units.” Start the timer.

2. Read aloud the physical setup shown on the worksheet: two point charges +q and –q separated by distance 2a, located on the x-axis, placed in a uniform electric field E pointing at angle θ above +x. Say: “We will calculate the dipole moment, the electric field at the midpoint by superposition, the flux through a small square, and the torque τ = p × E.”

3. While pairs work, circulate. For any pair that is stuck, prompt them to (a) identify q in coulombs, 2a in metres, and E in newtons per coulomb, (b) draw vectors for p and E on their worksheet, and (c) use the protractor to measure angle between p and E. If all pairs finish early, hand them the extension problem.

4. At 8 minutes, call the class back and ask two pairs to write their numerical answers for p (magnitude with units C·m), torque magnitude |τ| in N·m, and statement about net force on the dipole on the whiteboard. Congratulate correct unit-carrying answers and correct qualitative conclusion (net force zero in a uniform E).

5. If time allows (final minute), highlight on the whiteboard the derivation steps: p = q(2a) directed from −q to +q (units C·m), field at midpoint E_mid = E_+ + E_- by superposition (show signs), and magnitude |τ| = |p||E|sinφ where φ is angle from p to E (units N·m).
activities.title: Compute torque on a horizontal electric dipole in a uniform field

differentiation.extension: Compute the torque and net force if the external field is nonuniform: E(z)=E0(1 + α z) in the direction of the dipole axis (E0 in N/C, α in m^{-1}). Derive the net force as a function of α, q, and a, show units N, and evaluate numerically for given α so you can compare its magnitude to the torque found earlier.
differentiation.support: If you are stuck, use this sentence frame and worked first lines: "p = q·2a = (q value C)·(2a value m) = (compute) C·m. τ = p × E so |τ| = pE sinθ = (p number C·m)·(E number N/C)·sin(θ) = (compute) N·m. Direction: use right-hand rule: point fingers along p, curl to E, thumb gives τ direction." For the far-field: start by writing the field from +q at distance r - a ≈ r(1 - a/r) and from -q at r + a ≈ r(1 + a/r); expand each with first-order binomial approx to get the 1/r^2 cancellation and the remaining 1/r^3 term. Pair with a student who completed the example if you need help.

materials: one printed problem slip per pair (teacher prepares: values for q, a, r, and E)
student_instructions: Think (2 minutes, alone): Read your slip. Identify numeric q (in coulombs), a (in meters), p = q·(2a)·(direction) in C·m, the uniform field E (in N/C), and the far distance r (m). Calculate: (a) the torque vector τ = p × E (show magnitude in N·m and direction), (b) state whether a net force acts on the dipole in the uniform field and give one sentence justification using Coulomb's law, and (c) using Coulomb's law for the two charges, expand the field at a point on the dipole axis at distance r (with r >> a) to show how the leading term scales with 1/r^3; evaluate the numeric size of that field using the given numbers and include units.

Pair (4 minutes): Compare your calculations with your partner. Together write one neat torque calculation (with units) and one short derivation (3–5 lines) that shows the 1/r^3 dependence and the sign difference between the on-axis point (along the dipole axis) and an equatorial point (perpendicular to the dipole axis). Use k = 1/(4πϵ0) when converting constants to numbers. Be ready to write these on the board.
Share (when called): One partner will explain the torque calculation step-by-step and the other will explain the far-field derivation and the Gauss's law statement about net flux.
success_criteria: Each pair's written torque calculation shows τ = p × E with numeric magnitude in N·m and a correct direction (e.g., into or out of the page, given vector directions).

Each pair states clearly, in one sentence, that the net force on the dipole in a uniform E-field is zero and cites cancellation of Coulomb forces on the two charges (reference to equal magnitude, opposite direction).

At least one pair on the board produces a short algebraic expansion showing the leading dipole field term scales as 1/r^3 and identifies opposite signs on axis vs equatorial plane, with a numeric evaluation for their given r (units shown).
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in pairs. Hand each pair a printed problem slip that gives a dipole made of charges +q and -q separated by 2a, a numeric dipole moment p, a uniform external field E (magnitude and direction), and one far-field distance r where r >> a. Announce: "You will think individually for 2 minutes, discuss with your partner for 4 minutes, then we will share two answers in class for 6 minutes." Start the timer.

2. After 2 minutes, signal students to pair up and discuss. While they discuss (next 4 minutes), circulate. For each pair listen for (a) their calculation of torque magnitude and direction using τ = p × E with units N·m, (b) their statement about net force on the dipole in the uniform field with reasoning, and (c) their derivation showing how the dipole field at distance r depends on 1/r^3 and the sign difference on axis vs equatorial plane using given numeric values to show scale. Prompt pairs who are stuck with: "Show one force pair calculation from Coulomb's law and then combine them to get the dipole far-field scaling."

3. After 4 minutes of paired work, call the class together. Ask two different pairs to present: one pair to show their torque calculation step-by-step on the whiteboard (include units), and a second pair to show the short derivation that the far-field dipole potential/field falls as 1/r^3 and the sign change between on-axis and equatorial plane. Allow 3 minutes for the first presentation and 3 minutes for the second, correcting algebra or unit errors and reminding students to anchor symbols to numbers.

4. End by stating aloud the Gauss's law check: ask students to say whether the net flux through a large sphere enclosing the dipole is zero and why, and relate k = 1/(4πϵ0) when useful. Collect slips if you will grade them.
activities.title: Analyze a Small Electric Dipole in a Uniform Field and at Far Distance

differentiation.extension: Derive the electric field on the axis of a finite-length uniformly charged rod of total charge Q and length L at a point distance x from one end. Show all steps beginning from linear charge density λ = Q/L (units C/m), set up the integral for dQ, compute the integral, and state the limiting case as L → ∞ to recover the infinite-wire result. Carry units through the integral and result.
differentiation.support: If you are stuck, start with this worked example for the plane: Symmetry: field is perpendicular to plane. Gaussian surface: pillbox of face area A (m^2). Q_enclosed = σ·A (C). Flux = E·A (top) + E·A (bottom) = 2EA (units: (N/C)·m^2). Gauss: 2EA = Q_enclosed/ε0 = σA/ε0. Cancel A: E = σ/(2ε0). Units: [σ] = C/m^2, [ε0] = C^2·N^-1·m^-2 so E has units N/C. Pair weaker readers with a stronger reader and ask the stronger reader to read the worksheet steps aloud while the other follows along.

materials: printed worksheet with three blank derivation boxes (one per geometry) — 1 per pair
student_instructions: Work with your partner. Use Gauss's law: ∮ E·dA = Q_enclosed/ε0 and show every algebra step with units (SI units: ε0 in C^2·N^-1·m^-2 or equivalently C^2/(N·m^2)). Write answers on the worksheet boxes A, B, C.

Box A — Infinite uniformly charged plane (surface density σ in C/m^2): 1) State the symmetry and choose a Gaussian pillbox. 2) Write Q_enclosed = σ × area (include units C/m^2 × m^2 = C). 3) Compute flux = E × 2A (two faces), set equal to Q_enclosed/ε0 and solve for E. Show units for E (N/C or V/m).

Box B — Infinite straight wire (linear density λ in C/m): 1) State the symmetry and choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L. 2) Write Q_enclosed = λ × L (units: C/m × m = C). 3) Compute flux through curved surface = E(2π r L), set equal to Q_enclosed/ε0 and solve for E(r). Show direction and units for E.

Box C — Thin uniformly charged spherical shell (total charge Q in C or surface density σ in C/m^2): 1) For r outside the shell: choose a spherical Gaussian surface of radius r>R. Write Q_enclosed = Q (units C). Compute flux = E(4π r^2) and solve for E(r) showing units. 2) For r inside the shell (r<R): explain Q_enclosed = 0 and conclude E=0 with units.
At each derivation, explicitly label where superposition or symmetry was used and ensure every dQ expression shows correct SI units.
success_criteria: Each pair has a drawn Gaussian surface labeled (pillbox, cylinder, sphere) for the correct geometry visible on their worksheet.
Pairs have written the Q_enclosed expression with correct density symbol and units (e.g., Q = σ·A with units C/m^2·m^2 = C; Q = λ·L with units C).

Each pair reaches and writes the final expression for E with units: E_plane = σ/(2ε0) (N/C), E_wire = λ/(2π ε0 r) (N/C) or equivalent, E_shell_outside = Q/(4π ε0 r^2) (N/C), and E_shell_inside = 0 (N/C).
teacher_instructions: Group students in pairs. Hand each pair the printed worksheet and a calculator. Say: “In 8 minutes you will use Gauss’s law step by step to derive the electric field for three symmetric charge distributions: infinite plane, infinite straight wire, and thin spherical shell. Write each step with units.” Start the timer for 8 minutes.

Direct pairs to work in order: plane first (box A), then wire (box B), then spherical shell (box C). While they work, circulate and watch that each pair labels Gaussian surfaces, writes dQ expressions in terms of the given density (σ, λ, ρ as needed), carries SI units (C/m^2, C/m, C/m^3) and shows algebraic steps deriving E(r).
At 3 minutes remaining give an audible prompt: “Finish derivations and be ready to point to the step where you used symmetry and where you computed flux = E·A.”

When time is up, ask three pairs (one per geometry) to come to the board and quickly (1 minute each) point to and read aloud: (a) the Gaussian surface used and why, (b) the dQ expression with units, (c) the final formula with units. If any pair did not complete, ask them to underline the missing step on their worksheet.
activities.title: Derive fields from Gauss's Law: plane, wire, shell

items.answer: The electric field E at a point is defined operationally as the force F experienced per unit positive test charge q placed at that point: E = F/q (using a positive, negligibly small test charge so it does not disturb the source charges). Its SI unit is newtons per coulomb (N C^-1), which is equivalent to volts per metre (V m^-1).

rubric.criteria: Correct operational definition (force per unit positive test charge, test charge negligible) and correct SI unit with equivalent unit.

levels.descriptor: Gives the operational definition E = F/q with explicit statement that q is a positive, negligibly small test charge (so the source is not disturbed), and states the SI unit as N C^-1 and its equivalence V m^-1.
levels.label: Full credit

levels.descriptor: Gives E = F/q but omits that the test charge should be positive or negligibly small, or gives only one correct unit (either N C^-1 or V m^-1) without noting the equivalence.
levels.label: Partial credit

levels.descriptor: Definition incorrect or missing, and unit incorrect or missing.
levels.label: No credit

items.stem: State the operational definition of the electric field at a point in space using a test charge, and give its SI unit (including an equivalent unit).
items.working:
1. Definition: Place a small positive test charge q at the point; measure the force F on it. By definition E = F/q. This specifies the field as force per unit positive test charge and implies the test charge should be negligibly small so it does not disturb the source charge distribution.

2. Units: Force F has units N (newtons) and charge q has units C (coulombs), so E has units N/C.

3. Equivalence to V/m: 1 N = 1 kg·m·s^-2, and 1 volt V = 1 J/C = 1 (N·m)/C, so N/C = (N·m)/(C·m) = V/m. Therefore N C^-1 is equivalent to V m^-1.

items.answer: Approximately 0.216 N directed to the right (toward +x). Calculation: q1 = 3.0×10^-6 C, q2 = −2.0×10^-6 C, r = 0.50 m. |F| = k·|q1·q2|/r^2 = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2)(6.0×10^-12 C^2)/(0.50^2 m^2) ≈ 0.216 N. Opposite charges attract, so the force on q1 is toward q2 (to the right).

options.label: A
options.rationale: Correct: Convert charges to coulombs q1 = 3.0×10^-6 C, q2 = −2.0×10^-6 C. Magnitude = k·|q1·q2|/r^2 = (8.99×10^9)(6.0×10^-12)/(0.50^2) = (8.99×10^9)(2.4×10^-11) ≈ 0.216 N. Charges are opposite so they attract; q1 feels a force toward q2, i.e. to the right (+x). Units N are included.
options.text: Approximately 0.216 N directed to the right (toward +x), because opposite charges attract.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Wrong direction: While the magnitude 0.216 N is correct, the force is toward q2 (attraction), so it acts to the right. Saying left confuses sign of q1·q2 with the physical direction of attraction for opposite charges.

items.answer:
(a) Infinite plane (surface charge density σ, units C·m⁻²):
Symmetry: field is perpendicular to plane and same magnitude at equal distances on both sides. Choose a cylindrical Gaussian pillbox of cross-sectional area A (m²) whose flat faces are parallel to the plane and extend equally to both sides.
Gauss's law: ∮E·dA = Q_enclosed/ε0.
Flux through curved side = 0 (E perpendicular to curved side). Flux through two flat faces = E·A + E·A = 2EA.
Enclosed charge = σA.
So 2EA = σA/ε0 ⇒ E = σ/(2ε0). Direction: normal to the plane, away from plane if σ>0; toward plane if σ<0. Units: σ (C·m⁻²)/ε0 (C²·N⁻¹·m⁻²) gives E in N·C⁻¹ (or V·m⁻¹).

(b) Infinite line (linear charge density λ, units C·m⁻¹):
Symmetry: field is radial (perpendicular to wire) and depends only on radial distance r. Choose a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L (m).
Gauss's law: ∮E·dA = Q_enclosed/ε0.
Field is constant on curved surface and perpendicular to it, zero flux through end caps (field parallel to end caps). Flux = E(2πrL).
Enclosed charge = λL.
So E(2πrL) = λL/ε0 ⇒ E = λ/(2π ε0 r). Direction: radially outward for λ>0, inward for λ<0. Units: C·m⁻¹/(ε0·m) → N·C⁻¹.

(c) Thin spherical shell (total charge Q, radius R):
Symmetry: field is radial and depends only on r. Use a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius r and surface area 4πr².
Gauss's law: ∮E·dA = Q_enclosed/ε0.
(i) For r < R (interior): Gaussian surface encloses no charge (all charge on the shell). Q_enclosed = 0 ⇒ E(4πr²) = 0 ⇒ E = 0. Direction: zero field (no preferred direction).
(ii) For r > R (exterior): Gaussian surface encloses total charge Q. So E(4πr²) = Q/ε0 ⇒ E = Q/(4π ε0 r²). Direction: radial (away from centre if Q>0). This equals the field of a point charge Q at the centre. Units: C/(ε0·m²) → N·C⁻¹.

In all parts ε0 is the vacuum permittivity (ε0 ≈ 8.85×10⁻¹² C²·N⁻¹·m⁻²).

items.stem:
Use Gauss's law to derive expressions for the electric field magnitude and direction in the following three cases. In each part state the Gaussian surface you choose, the symmetry argument that justifies it, and show the algebraic steps that lead to the final formula (include units for physical constants and clearly state what each symbol means).

(a) An infinite plane with uniform surface charge density σ (C·m⁻²). Give E for points on either side of the plane.

(b) An infinitely long straight wire with uniform linear charge density λ (C·m⁻¹). Give E at a distance r from the wire (r measured perpendicular to the wire).

(c) A uniformly charged thin spherical shell of total charge Q (C) and radius R. Give E for (i) r < R (interior points) and (ii) r > R (exterior points), where r is the radial distance from the centre.
items.working:
(a) Infinite plane:
1. Choose pillbox with area A. By symmetry E normal to plane and same magnitude on both faces.
2. Flux = E·A (top) + E·A (bottom) = 2EA.
3. Q_enclosed = σA.
4. Gauss: 2EA = σA/ε0 ⇒ cancel A ⇒ E = σ/(2ε0). Units N·C⁻¹.

(b) Infinite line:
1. Choose coaxial cylinder radius r length L. By symmetry E radial and constant on curved surface.
2. Flux through curved surface = E·(2πrL). End caps contribute zero.
3. Q_enclosed = λL.
4. Gauss: E(2πrL) = λL/ε0 ⇒ cancel L ⇒ E = λ/(2π ε0 r). Units N·C⁻¹.

(c) Spherical shell:
1. Choose concentric sphere radius r. By symmetry E radial and constant over sphere.
2. Flux = E·(4πr²).
3. (i) r < R: Q_enclosed = 0 ⇒ E(4πr²) = 0 ⇒ E = 0.
4. (ii) r > R: Q_enclosed = Q ⇒ E(4πr²) = Q/ε0 ⇒ E = Q/(4π ε0 r²). Units N·C⁻¹.
5. Note: ε0 ≈ 8.85×10⁻¹² C²·N⁻¹·m⁻².

The elementary charge of an electron is e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C (negative for electrons). Two neutral insulating objects A and B are rubbed together so that 2.0 × 10^12 electrons are transferred from A to B.

(a) Calculate the net electric charge on object A and on object B after the transfer. Give your answers with correct signs and units. (2 marks)

(b) Explain, using the microscopic origin of charge, why (i) the net charge on each object is an integer multiple of e and (ii) the total charge of the isolated two-object system is conserved. Briefly address the common misconception that rubbing 'creates' new charge. (2 marks)
items.working:
(a) Number of electrons transferred: N = 2.0 × 10^12 (dimensionless).
Charge per electron: e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C (magnitude).
Charge moved (magnitude) = N × e = (2.0 × 10^12)(1.60 × 10^-19 C) = 3.20 × 10^-7 C.
Object A loses N electrons, so its net charge Q_A = + (N e) = +3.20 × 10^-7 C.
Object B gains N electrons, so its net charge Q_B = - (N e) = -3.20 × 10^-7 C.
Check conservation: Q_total = Q_A + Q_B = +3.20 × 10^-7 C + (−3.20 × 10^-7 C) = 0 C.

(b) Microscopic origin: electrons (charge −e) and protons (charge +e) are discrete. Any change in net charge equals an integer number of these charge carriers multiplied by e, so charges are quantised. Rubbing moves electrons from one body to the other; it does not create or destroy electron/proton pairs in this isolated system, so total charge is conserved.

items.answer:
All three phenomena are discharges of static electric charge caused by a build-up of charge (usually excess electrons or a net positive deficit of electrons) and a later rapid movement of charge to neutralise a potential difference.

(a) Synthetic jumper spark: When you pull off or rub a synthetic jumper, friction causes transfer of electrons between the fibres and your body (triboelectric effect). The body or jumper becomes charged, producing a potential difference of order 1 000–3 000 V relative to surrounding objects. If the potential difference is large enough across a small gap, the air breaks down and a tiny spark (a brief flow of electrons) jumps, equalising the charge. The spark is short (millimetres) and produces a small shock and sometimes a visible snap and smell of ozone.

(b) Shock from a metal door handle after walking on carpet: Walking across carpet causes repeated contact and separation between shoe soles and carpet fibres, transferring charge so your body can accumulate a net charge (often negative). A metal handle is a good conductor and provides a path to ground. When you reach and touch the handle, the potential difference between your charged body and the handle causes electrons to move quickly through the small contact gap — a discharge you feel as a small shock. Typical voltages producing felt shocks are around 1 000–3 000 V; the actual charge is small, so the energy is low but enough to be felt.

(c) Lightning: In storm clouds, collisions between ice particles and water droplets separate charges so large regions of a cloud become strongly charged (positive and negative regions). The potential difference between cloud and ground (or between cloud regions) can reach tens to hundreds of millions of volts (≈10^7–10^9 V). When the electric field exceeds air breakdown (roughly 3 × 10^6 V m^-1), a conductive channel forms and a huge current flows — the lightning stroke — rapidly neutralising charge over kilometres and releasing large energy, heat, light, and thunder.

Common mechanism: In all cases charge separation creates a potential difference; when the local electric field exceeds the breakdown threshold of air (or a conductive path is provided), rapid movement of charge (a discharge) occurs. The main differences are scale (small sparks: ~10^3 V, short gaps; lightning: ~10^7–10^9 V, long channels) and energy delivered (small shocks have very low energy; lightning releases very large energy).

items.working:
Given q1 = +6.0 μC = 6.0 × 10^-6 C, q2 = +2.0 μC = 2.0 × 10^-6 C, r = 0.50 m, k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2.
Coulomb's law: F = k |q1 q2| / r^2.
Compute product of charges: q1 q2 = (6.0 × 10^-6 C)(2.0 × 10^-6 C) = 12.0 × 10^-12 C^2 = 1.20 × 10^-11 C^2.
Compute r^2 = (0.50 m)^2 = 0.25 m^2.
Compute F = (8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2) × (1.20 × 10^-11 C^2) / (0.25 m^2)

Since both charges are positive, like charges repel. Therefore the force is repulsive. The force on the +6.0 μC sphere is directed away from the +2.0 μC sphere along the line joining them.

items.answer:
(a) Infinite plane (surface charge density sigma): Choose a cylindrical pillbox that intersects the plane, with flat faces of area A, one face on each side of the plane. By symmetry E is perpendicular to the plane and equal in magnitude on both sides.

Gauss's law: \Phi = \oint E·dA = E·A (top) + E·A (bottom) = 2EA = Q_enc/epsilon_0 = (sigma A)/epsilon_0.

Therefore E = sigma/(2 epsilon_0), directed normal to the plane, away from the plane if sigma>0.

(b) Infinite straight wire (linear charge density lambda): Choose a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L. By symmetry E is radial and constant on the curved surface; flux through end caps is zero.

Gauss's law: \Phi = E (2 pi r L) = Q_enc/epsilon_0 = (lambda L)/epsilon_0.

Therefore E = lambda/(2 pi epsilon_0 r), directed radially outward if lambda>0.

(c) Thin spherical shell (radius R, total charge Q): Choose a spherical Gaussian surface of radius r centered on the shell.

- For r>R (outside): symmetry gives E radial and constant on sphere of area 4 pi r^2.

Gauss's law: E (4 pi r^2) = Q/epsilon_0 => E = Q/(4 pi epsilon_0 r^2), directed radially outward if Q>0. (Same as a point charge Q at center.)

- For r<R (inside): the Gaussian sphere encloses no charge (Q_enc = 0), so E (4 pi r^2) = 0 => E = 0 for r<R.

items.stem:
Use Gauss's law to derive expressions for the magnitude and direction of the electric field for each of the following charge distributions. In each case state the Gaussian surface you choose and give the final answer in terms of the given charge density and epsilon_0.

(a) An infinite uniformly charged plane with surface charge density sigma (C m^-2).
(b) An infinitely long straight wire with linear charge density lambda (C m^-1). Give the field at radial distance r from the wire axis.
(c) A uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius R with total charge Q. Give the field for r<R (inside) and for r>R (outside).
items.working:
(a) Infinite plane

Choose a thin cylindrical pillbox symmetric about the plane, face area A (m^2). Surface charge density sigma (C m^-2) means charge enclosed Q_enc = sigma A (C).

Flux: \Phi = E_top A + E_bottom A = 2 E A  (E constant on faces, field parallel to area normals)

Gauss's law: 2 E A = Q_enc/epsilon_0 = (sigma A)/epsilon_0  => E = sigma/(2 epsilon_0).

Units: sigma in C m^-2, epsilon_0 in C^2 N^-1 m^-2 (or equivalently C^2/(N m^2)), so E in N C^-1 (V m^-1).

(b) Infinite straight wire

Choose a cylinder coaxial with the wire, radius r (m), length L (m). Linear charge density lambda (C m^-1) gives Q_enc = lambda L (C).

Flux: only curved surface contributes: \Phi = E (2 pi r L).

Gauss's law: E (2 pi r L) = Q_enc/epsilon_0 = (lambda L)/epsilon_0  => E = lambda/(2 pi epsilon_0 r).

Units: lambda in C m^-1, so E in N C^-1 as above.

(c) Thin spherical shell

Choose spherical Gaussian surface radius r.

If r > R: Q_enc = Q. Flux: E (4 pi r^2) = Q/epsilon_0  => E = Q/(4 pi epsilon_0 r^2). Units: Q (C), r (m).

If r < R: Q_enc = 0 (no charge inside shell). Flux: E (4 pi r^2) = 0 => E = 0.

These results assume electrostatic equilibrium, perfect symmetry, and that the plane/wire are effectively infinite so edge effects are negligible.

items.answer: Rubbing transfers electrons (each with charge −e = −1.60×10^-19 C) from one rod to the other so each rod’s net charge is an integer multiple of e; the total charge of the two-rod system remains constant because no net charge is created or destroyed. Direction: field points toward the negative charge; at the midpoint (left of the −2.0 μC) this is also to the right.
Because both fields point to the right, they add:
E_total = E_+ + E_- = 1.15072×10^6 + 2.8768×10^5 = 1.4384×10^6 N/C ≈ 1.44×10^6 N/C to the right.
Force on the test charge q_test = +1.0 μC = 1.0×10^−6 C:
F = q_test × E_total = (1.0×10^−6 C) × (1.4384×10^6 N/C) = 1.4384 N ≈ 1.44 N to the right.
(Units carried through: N/C × C = N.)

items.answer:

items.stem: Air breaks down and produces a spark when the electric field exceeds about 3.0 × 10^6 V/m. (a) Calculate the voltage difference needed to produce a spark across a 1.0 cm gap (typical spark between synthetic clothes). (b) Calculate the voltage difference needed to produce a spark across a 2.0 mm gap (typical small shock when touching a metal handle). (c) Based on your calculations, state which spark requires the larger voltage and give one everyday reason why one type of spark is more common than the other. (Use 3.0 × 10^6 V/m for the breakdown strength of air. Give answers with correct units.)
items.working:
(a) Convert gap to metres: 1.0 cm = 0.010 m.
Use V = E × d where E = 3.0 × 10^6 V/m.
V = (3.0 × 10^6 V/m) × (0.010 m) = 3.0 × 10^4 V = 30 000 V = 30 kV.

(b) Convert gap to metres: 2.0 mm = 0.0020 m.
V = (3.0 × 10^6 V/m) × (0.0020 m) = 6.0 × 10^3 V = 6 000 V = 6.0 kV.

(c) Compare: 30 kV (1.0 cm) is greater than 6.0 kV (2.0 mm), so the 1.0 cm spark requires the larger voltage. Everyday reason: smaller gaps need less charge/voltage to reach breakdown, so small shocks occur more often; building up 30 kV for a 1 cm spark is less common than the few kilovolts needed for a tiny spark.

teacher_script.speaker_notes: Hand out a 2-question quiz (or show it on the board): Q1 (calculation): "Two point charges +1.0×10⁻6 C and +2.0×10⁻6 C separated by 0.15 m. Compute magnitude of force and state units." Q2 (concept): "If an isolated neutral object is rubbed and becomes +3.2×10⁻7 C, did rubbing create charge? Explain in one sentence mentioning electrons or protons." Give one minute to answer Q1 and one minute to answer Q2. Collect answers quickly (or have volunteers read). Give the correct brief answers: show numeric answer for Q1 and the conservation answer for Q2. Force ∝ 1/r^2 (Coulomb)
Definition (exact): The vector field produced by a charge that exerts force on other charges placed in the surrounding space.
Operational definition (exact): E(r) = lim_{q->0} F/q, the force per unit test charge in the limit of negligible test charge.
Units of E: N/C (force N per charge C)
Demo: r = 0.20 m ; q_test = +1.0×10^-6 C ; measured F = 0.012 N → E = 1.2×10^4 N/C (radially away)
Example A: Q = +5.0 μC, r = 0.50 m → E = 1.80×10^5 N/C, radially away
Example B: Q = −3.0 μC, r = 0.20 m → E = 6.74×10^5 N/C, radially toward source
Remember: F(r) = q E(r)
Next: superposition of fields (sum of point-charge fields)

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The electric field is the force per unit positive test charge (E = F/q) measured in newtons per coulomb (N/C).
checkpoint_questions.question: State the operational definition of the electric field in one sentence and give its SI unit.
A point charge Q = +5.0 μC produces a force of 0.045 N on a +1.0 μC test charge at a certain point. Use the operational definition to find the electric field magnitude at that point (show units).

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: (a) For Q = +3.0 μC, E points radially away from the charge (r̂) because a positive test charge is repelled. (b) For Q = −3.0 μC, E points radially toward the charge (−r̂) because a positive test charge is attracted.
checkpoint_questions.question: Using E(r) = (1/4πε0) Q / r^2 r̂, indicate the direction of E at distance r from (a) Q = +3.0 μC and (b) Q = −3.0 μC. Give a one-line justification for each.

entry_ticket.expected_response: E = 0.020 N/C to the right. Explanation: electric field = force on a +test charge divided by that test charge, here the charge is 1 (so force per unit test charge = 0.020 N/C to the right).
entry_ticket.prompt: Write a one-sentence answer on your paper: If a small positive test charge at a point feels a force of 0.020 N to the right, what is the electric field at that point? Give a number, unit, and direction. (No calculator needed.)

exit_ticket.prompt: Part A (short): Write the operational definition of electric field and its SI unit. Part B (calculation): Compute the magnitude and direction of the electric field at r = 0.20 m from a point charge Q = −2.0 μC. Show units and state the direction relative to the source charge.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Part A names E as force per unit positive test charge and gives unit N/C. Part B calculates E = (1/4πε0)·|Q|/r^2 numerically (≈ value in N/C with units) and states that the field points toward the negative source charge (radially inward).

tasks: 1) Compute the electric field magnitude and direction at r = 0.10 m and r = 0.50 m from a point charge Q = +4.0 μC. Show all steps, carry units (N/C) through, and write answers with direction (radially away/toward).

2) A small test probe measures a force of 0.012 N when placed 0.15 m from an unknown point charge. If the probe is +2.0 μC, find the source charge Q (include sign) using F = qE and E from the point-charge formula. Show units and reasoning.
3) Short conceptual: Explain in two sentences why the test charge must be 'negligibly small' when defining the electric field.

mentor_moment.story: In a lab, a student used a relatively large test sphere and found different force readings at different probe sizes. Shrinking the probe to a tiny bead removed the discrepancy because the smaller probe disturbed the source charge far less.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Make your test charge small so it measures the field without changing it; always report units (N/C) when you quote E.

teacher_script.heading: Quick review and activation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Class, take out a scrap of paper. Put your name on it. Read the prompt at the top and write one short line with a number, a unit and a direction. Do it now." Pause 30 seconds. Then say: "Who wrote 0.020 N/C to the right? Raise your hand." Point to one student and ask them to read their answer aloud. Then say: "Two quick recall questions: 1) What are the SI units of force and charge?" Wait for responses (N and C). 2) "How does Coulomb force depend on distance between two point charges?" Wait for answer (inverse-square). Conclude: "Good — we will use those facts now to define electric field."

What is r̂ exactly — how do I show its direction?

teacher_script.board_action: Write the sourced definitions exactly: 'The vector field produced by a charge that exerts force on other charges placed in the surrounding space.' and 'E(r) = lim_{q->0} F/q, the force per unit test charge in the limit of negligible test charge.' Then write the formula: 'E = (1/4πε0) Q / r^2 r̂' and below it 'Units: N/C'.
teacher_script.heading: Derive E = F/q_test from Coulomb's law
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Hold up the script and say exactly: "We start with a point source charge Q at the origin and a small positive test charge q_test placed a distance r to the right. Using Coulomb's law, the force on q_test is F = (1/4πε0) Q q_test / r^2 in the radial direction. Now divide both sides by q_test and speak each step as I write it. I will write: E(r) = F / q_test = (1/4πε0) Q / r^2 r̂. Say this with me: 'Electric field is force per unit positive test charge.' Note units: force is N, divide by charge in C, so E has unit N/C. Also show the alternative unit N·m/C when multiplied back by q to get force — but keep N/C as the unit of E. Now read aloud the operational definition from the source: 'E(r) = lim_{q->0} F/q, the force per unit test charge in the limit of negligible test charge.' Emphasize: the test charge must be small so it does not move the source charge."

teacher_script.board_action: Write the measurement: 'demo: r = 0.20 m ; q_test = +1.0×10^-6 C ; measured F = 0.012 N' and the calculation 'E = 0.012 N / 1.0×10^-6 C = 1.2×10^4 N/C (radially away)'.
teacher_script.heading: Demonstration: measure force and compute E
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "I will show you a small demo. I have two conducting spheres fixed in place; one is connected to the high-voltage supply and will be our source charge Q. I will bring a tiny probe (a small pith ball on an insulating rod or a calibrated force sensor) to a measured distance r from the source, record the force, and compute E = F/q_test. Watch and copy the numbers I call out." Proceed: place probe at r = 0.20 m from the center of the charged sphere. Announce: "The probe's charge is q_test = +1.0 μC = 1.0×10^-6 C (we prepared it). The force sensor reads F = 0.012 N away from the source." Write each number as you say it. Then compute aloud step by step: "E = F / q_test = 0.012 N / (1.0×10^-6 C) = 1.2×10^4 N/C radially away (point right if the probe is on the right)." Ask: "Does this E depend on the fact that the probe's actual q_test was 1.0 μC? If I used 0.5 μC and recorded half the force, would E change?" Wait for answers and say: "No — E is independent of q_test in the ideal limit."

anticipated_questions: Why did we drop the sign when computing magnitude?
Do we need to include vector arrows on numbers?

teacher_script.board_action: Write Example A full calculation and result: 'Q = +5.0×10^-6 C ; r = 0.50 m ; E = 1.80×10^5 N/C, radially away (r̂)'. Write Example B set-up: 'Q = −3.0×10^-6 C ; r = 0.20 m' and leave space for student work. After checking, write the computed result 'E = 6.74×10^5 N/C, radially toward source (−r̂)'.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice: two worked examples in pairs
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Turn to a partner. We'll do two short calculations together — I'll do the first with you, then you do the second and I'll check. Example A: source Q = +5.0 μC, find E at r = 0.50 m. Steps to say and write aloud with me: convert Q to coulombs Q = +5.0×10^-6 C. Compute magnitude using E = (1/4πε0) Q / r^2. Use 1/4πε0 = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. So E = 8.99×10^9 × 5.0×10^-6 / (0.50^2) N/C. Calculate: numerator = 8.99×10^9 × 5.0×10^-6 = 4.495×10^4 N·m^2/C, divide by 0.25 m^2 gives E = 1.798×10^5 N/C. Direction: because Q is positive, E points radially away from Q (explicitly write r̂)." Pause while pairs copy. Then say: "Example B (your turn): Q = −3.0 μC at r = 0.20 m. Compute magnitude and give direction. I will come around." Circulate and check one pair's work: expected magnitude calculation steps: Q = −3.0×10^-6 C, E = 8.99×10^9 × 3.0×10^-6 / (0.20^2) = (8.99×10^9×3.0×10^-6)/(0.04) = (2.697×10^4)/0.04 = 6.7425×10^5 N/C. Direction: towards the charge because Q is negative (write −r̂ or 'towards source').

teacher_script.heading: Check, short quiz and summary
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Turn your papers back to me. Two-minute quiz: answer three items on the sheet I'll hand out. Item 1 (concept): If a test charge placed at a point experiences a force opposite to the electric field direction, was the test charge positive or negative? Write one word. Item 2 (numeric): A +2.0×10^-6 C test charge feels a force of 0.040 N toward the left. What is E? Give number, unit and direction. Item 3 (short): Why must the test charge be 'negligibly small'?" Hand out or display the items and give 2 minutes. Collect answers quickly. Then speak a 30-second summary: read aloud the exact definition from the source once more: 'The vector field produced by a charge that exerts force on other charges placed in the surrounding space.' Remind them of the formula they must remember: F(r)=q E(r) and E(point) = (1/4πε0) q / r^2 r̂, units N/C. Finish: "Next period we'll add fields from more than one charge using superposition."

bullet_points: Point-charge field: E = (1/4πε0) q / r^2 · r̂    (units: N/C)
Superposition: E(r) = Σ_i (1/4πε0) q_i / r_iP^2 · r̂_iP
Electric flux (definition): dΦ = E · dS = E dS cosθ    (units: (N/C)·m^2)
Electric dipole: two charges +q and −q separated by 2a. Total charge = 0.
Dipole moment (definition): p = q × 2 a  (vector from − to +, units C·m)
Force on each charge in uniform E: magnitude F = q E  (units N)
Torque derivation (steps):
torque from one charge = q E · (a sinθ)  (N·m)
total τ = 2 (q E a sinθ) = (2 q a) E sinθ
substitute p = 2 q a → τ (magnitude) = p E sinθ    (units N·m)
Vector form (statement): τ = p × E    (direction by right-hand rule)
Key point: Net force on neutral dipole in uniform E = 0 N (forces cancel).
diagrams_to_draw: Two positive charges example: +2.0 μC at x=−0.10 m and +2.0 μC at x=+0.10 m; arrows showing fields at origin cancel.
Dipole diagram: −q (left) and +q (right) separated by 2a, centre marked, p arrow from − to +, show angle θ between p and uniform E (E arrow to right).
Show forces on each charge: F_on_+ = +q E (arrow right), F_on_- = −q E (arrow left), show lever arms a and perpendicular component a sinθ, indicate torque sense.
headings: Torque on dipole in uniform E (derivation)

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Magnitude p = q·(2a) where q = 3.0×10^-6 C and separation 2a = 0.04 m, so p = 3.0×10^-6 C × 0.04 m = 1.2×10^-7 C·m. Direction: from negative to positive charge, i.e. +x direction. So p = (1.2×10^-7 C·m) x̂.
checkpoint_questions.question: Two point charges +3.0 μC and -3.0 μC are separated by 4.0 cm along the x-axis, with the negative charge at x = 0 and the positive at x = 0.04 m. What is the dipole moment vector p (magnitude, direction, and units)?
A dipole with p = 2.0×10^-7 C·m lies in a uniform electric field E = 5.0×10^3 N/C at angle θ = 30° between p and E. Calculate the magnitude of the torque τ and give units.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: No net force. Each charge experiences an equal-magnitude force in opposite directions when the field is uniform (F+ = qE, F- = -qE), so vector sum F_total = qE + (-qE) = 0 N. Superposition of the two point-charge forces gives zero net force.
checkpoint_questions.question: A dipole (total charge zero) is placed in a perfectly uniform electric field. Will the dipole experience a net force? Briefly justify your answer using superposition.

entry_ticket.expected_response: Net force = 0 N (because +q and −q feel equal and opposite forces in a uniform field). Net torque ≠ 0 N·m in general: torque tends to rotate the dipole; for example if the line joining charges is at angle θ to E, torque magnitude = p E sinθ with units N·m, where p (dipole moment) = q·2a (units C·m).
entry_ticket.prompt: Two point charges +q and −q are fixed 2a apart (negative on the left, positive on the right). The pair is placed in a uniform electric field E pointing to the right. In one short sentence, write the net force on the pair and the net torque on the pair (include units).

exit_ticket.prompt: A dipole consists of +4.0 μC and −4.0 μC separated by 6.0 cm, with the negative charge at the origin and the positive at x = 0.06 m. It sits in a uniform electric field E = 1.0×10^4 N/C directed at 60° above the +x axis. Calculate (a) the dipole moment vector p (include units and direction), (b) the torque vector τ (magnitude, direction relative to the page), and (c) whether a net force acts on the dipole (show the reasoning in one sentence).
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Student calculates p = q·2a = (4.0×10^-6 C)(0.06 m) = 2.4×10^-7 C·m directed +x; computes τ = p×E giving magnitude τ = pE sin60° ≈ (2.4×10^-7)(1.0×10^4)·(√3/2) ≈ 2.08×10^-3 N·m; states torque direction is out-of-plane (use right-hand rule: into or out of page consistent with p×E) and correctly states net force = 0 N because +q and −q forces cancel in a uniform E.

homework.submission_format: Handwritten work or scanned PDF with calculations and units shown; label final answers clearly with units.
tasks: Compute the dipole moment (magnitude and direction) for each: (a) +2.0 μC and −2.0 μC separated by 2.0 cm along y, (b) +5.0 μC and −5.0 μC separated by 10 cm making a 45° line in the xy-plane (show vector components in C·m).

For the dipole in (b) above and a uniform field E = 2.0×10^3 N/C pointing along +x, calculate the torque vector (components and magnitude, include units) and state whether a net force acts. Show the algebraic steps and carry units through every line.
Short conceptual: Explain in 2–3 sentences why a non-uniform external electric field can produce a net force on a dipole while a uniform field cannot.

mentor_moment.story: In lab, a student placed a charged bead pair in a uniform field expecting it to drift. Instead it only rotated until aligned with the field. They realised equal opposite forces cancel while the off-axis push makes a twist.
mentor_moment.takeaway: When total charge is zero, think 'rotation, not translation' — uniform fields give torque (p×E) but no net force.
mentor_moment.title: Lab paddle surprise

anticipated_questions: Why do the fields cancel instead of add? (Because directions are opposite at the origin.)
Do we need to use components? (Yes when directions differ; here they are opposite on the same line.)
What value for 1/4πε0 should we use? (Use 9.0×10^9 N·m^2/C^2 for quick estimates.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the point-charge field formula and the two-charge superposition sum. Show the numeric substitution and cancellation.
teacher_script.heading: Activate prior knowledge — quick review and worked example
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Quick review: write the electric field from a single point charge q at distance r. Include units." Pause while one student writes. Then point: "That field has units N/C and depends on 1/r^2. Now a quick worked example: two equal positive charges +2.0 μC at x = −0.10 m and +2.0 μC at x = +0.10 m. What is the electric field at the origin (x=0)?" Ask a volunteer to compute with you on the board. Guide calculation: compute magnitude from each charge using E = (1/4πε0) q / r^2, show numbers: q = 2.0×10^-6 C, r = 0.10 m, (1/4πε0) ≈ 9.0×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. Compute each E in N/C, show directions (both point away from each positive charge) and add vectors by superposition to get net E at origin (they cancel so net E = 0 N/C). Emphasise units N/C and that we add vectors component-wise."

anticipated_questions: Why is p from negative to positive? (This is the chosen convention from the source; it matches the field direction on the axis at far distances.)
Is p a vector or scalar? (p is a vector; include direction and units C·m.)
What does flux physically mean? (Proportional to number of field lines crossing; units (N/C)·m^2.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the dipole moment definition, the sample numeric computation for p with units, and the electric flux definition with units.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce electric dipole and dipole moment; define electric flux
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now a dipole: take two charges +q and −q separated by distance 2a. The pair is called an electric dipole. I will write the definition we must use." Read aloud the source definition for dipole moment. Then write p = q × 2 a and say: "This is a vector from the negative charge to the positive charge. Units: C·m." Next: "Write the electric flux definition exactly as given." Write dΦ = E · dS = E dS cosθ and say: "Units for flux are (N/C)·m^2. dS is a vector whose magnitude is area in m^2 and whose direction is normal to the surface; for a closed surface dS points outward." Show a quick numeric example: q = 3.0 μC, 2a = 0.20 m, compute p magnitude = q·2a = (3.0×10^-6 C)(0.20 m) = 6.0×10^-7 C·m and write the calculation and units on the board."

anticipated_questions: Why multiply by 2? (Because both charges produce torques that add.)
Should we use cross product or scalar magnitude? (We use both: magnitude is pE sinθ; vector form is p × E.)
What happens if field is not uniform? (Then forces on the two charges need not cancel — outside today's scope but point out the reason.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw dipole in E field with forces labelled (F = qE, direction shown), show distances a, label angle θ between p and E, write algebraic steps: τ = 2 (qE)(a sinθ) → τ = (2 q a) E sinθ → τ = p E sinθ, then write vector statement τ = p × E and note units N·m.
teacher_script.heading: Demonstration: dipole in uniform electric field and computing torque
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Set up or draw the apparatus: show two charges +q (right) and −q (left) separated by 2a mounted on a short rigid rod that can rotate, placed in uniform E pointing to the right. Say: "Point out the forces on each charge: F = qE, direction depends on sign. Write the two forces as vectors and show they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction if the dipole axis is perpendicular to E, but generally produce a couple that creates torque." Draw forces on the diagram: on +q force to the right, on −q force to the left. Next compute the torque step-by-step for the general case where the dipole axis makes angle θ with E: write force magnitudes F = qE (units N). Show lever arms: each force acts at distance a from the center, perpendicular component = a sinθ. Compute torque magnitude from one force as τ_one = qE · a sinθ, total torque = 2·(qE a sinθ) = (2 q a) E sinθ. Substitute p = q·2a and conclude torque magnitude τ = p E sinθ (units N·m). Say: "Vector form: τ = p × E, direction given by right-hand rule." Walk students through units to show N·m. Emphasise no net force in a uniform field because forces cancel.

anticipated_questions: Do we include units in each step? (Yes: show C·m for p and N·m for torque.)
How to get the sine value? (Use sin30° = 0.5; calculators OK.)
How to decide clockwise or anticlockwise? (Use the picture: if p is above E and needs to rotate down, say which direction that is in the diagram.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the two problems, then write the worked numeric solutions with units shown step-by-step for p and τ and label direction of rotation.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice in pairs — computations
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Give two short problems on the board and ask pairs to work for 6 minutes, then discuss answers: Problem (a): q = 4.0×10^-6 C, separation 2a = 0.30 m. Compute p (include units). Problem (b): For the dipole from (a) in a uniform E = 5.0×10^3 N/C, with the dipole axis at θ = 30° to E, compute the torque magnitude and state its direction (clockwise or anticlockwise when viewed from above). Circulate, check units and arithmetic. After 6 minutes, select a pair to present their numeric steps: (a) p = q·2a = (4.0×10^-6 C)(0.30 m) = 1.2×10^-6 C·m. (b) τ = p E sinθ = (1.2×10^-6 C·m)(5.0×10^3 N/C) sin30° = compute: 1.2×10^-6×5.0×10^3 = 6.0×10^-3; ×0.5 = 3.0×10^-3 N·m. Explain direction using right-hand rule: if p points from − to + and angle is 30° above E, torque tries to rotate p toward alignment with E — name clockwise/anticlockwise based on diagram."

anticipated_questions: What if charges are different? (Then not a pure dipole; total charge not zero and a net force can appear.)
Is the torque calculation different for θ = 0 or 180°? (Yes: sin0°=0 so torque = 0.)
What if dipole is in a non-uniform field? (We only state that net force can occur then; not computed today.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the three check questions on the board for students to copy, and after sampling, write the correct brief answers and numerical torque with units: τ = p E sin90° = (2.0×10^-6)(1.0×10^4)(1) = 2.0×10^-2 N·m.
teacher_script.heading: Check for understanding — three quick concept checks
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Read three short questions aloud and have students write single-line answers on a slip: (1) Does a dipole in a uniform E experience a net force? Answer and units. (2) Why does zero net charge imply no net force in a uniform E? One-sentence explanation. (3) Compute the torque numerically for this quick case: p = 2.0×10^-6 C·m, E = 1.0×10^4 N/C, θ = 90° (units). Give 90 seconds for answers, then sample 3 students' answers aloud and correct any errors immediately. Emphasise unit consistency in the numerical answer (N·m)."

anticipated_questions: Will we need formulas for the dipole field next class? (Yes — we'll derive far-field forms using p.)
Do we always use p = q·2a or is there a sign? (p is a vector from negative to positive; magnitude is q·2a.)
Should we memorise the torque formula? (Understand the derivation and the units; you will use it next time.)
teacher_script.board_action: Underline the final boxed results: p = q·2a (C·m), dΦ = E·dS (units), τ = p E sinθ (units N·m) and the note: Net force = 0 in uniform E for neutral dipole.
teacher_script.heading: Consolidate results and bridge to next period
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Summarise aloud while pointing to the board: "We used superposition to combine point-charge fields, defined dipole and dipole moment p = q·2a (C·m), and defined electric flux dΦ = E·dS with units (N/C)·m^2. We derived the torque on a dipole in a uniform E: magnitude τ = p E sinθ and vector form τ = p × E with units N·m. Net force in a uniform field is zero for a neutral dipole. Next time we will use p to describe the dipole's far-field behaviour and connect to Gauss's law and Coulomb's law. Make sure your notes include units at every step." End with: "Any final quick questions?" then collect slips or record common errors to address next period.

bullet_points: Coulomb constant: k = 1/(4πε0) with units N·m^2/C^2
Dipole moment: p (vector) = q · d (C·m). For two charges ±q separated by 2a, magnitude p = q·(2a).
Units to watch: q in C, a and r in m, p in C·m, E in N/C, τ in N·m
Axis point: P at x = r (r ≫ a). Leading nonzero term after cancellation ∝ qa / r^3 → substitute p = q·(2a)
Equatorial point: leading field ∝ −qa / r^3 → substitute p

Sketch: equatorial point P on y-axis at y=r with same dipole along x. Show field direction opposite to p.
Demonstration set-up: two small spheres separated by 2a on a rotatable bar between parallel plates producing E.
