checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Compute cross product: p (4.0 î) × E (0.50 ĵ) = (4.0×0.50)(î×ĵ) = 2.0 k̂. So τ = 2.0 N·m in the +z direction (written 2.0 k̂ N·m).
checkpoint_questions.question: A dipole has p = 4.0 C·m pointing in +x. It sits in a uniform field E = 0.50 N/C in the +y direction. What is the torque vector τ = p × E (include units and sign)?

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Net force = 0 because forces on +q and −q are equal in magnitude and opposite, so they cancel. Units: force in newtons (N); torque in newton-meters (N·m).
checkpoint_questions.question: Is there any net force on an ideal electric dipole placed in a strictly uniform electric field? Give one-sentence explanation and state the units you would use for the net force and for torque.

On the axis of a dipole at large distance r the field scales like 1/r^3. If the field at r = 1.0 m is 8.0×10−6 N/C, what is the field at r = 2.0 m (same axis)? Show the quick calculation and give units.

entry_ticket.expected_response: Circle: 1/r^3. Short reason: At distances r ≫ a the fields from +q and −q mostly cancel their 1/r^2 pieces and the leading term falls off faster, as 1/r^3; this is why a dipole's field decreases faster than a single charge's field.
entry_ticket.prompt: Quick pick (2 minutes). For a point charge the electric field magnitude falls as 1/r^2. For an electric dipole (two equal opposite charges ±q separated by 2a) at distances r much larger than a, which of these is the correct dependence of the dipole field magnitude on r? Circle one: 1/r, 1/r^2, 1/r^3, 1/r^4. Write the letter and one short reason (one sentence).

exit_ticket.prompt: A small ideal dipole has dipole moment p = (2.0 î − 3.0 ĵ) C·m. It is placed in a uniform field E = (0.40 ĵ + 0.30 k̂) N/C. (a) Calculate the torque vector τ = p × E with units. (b) State whether a net force acts on the dipole and give a one-line justification including units for force.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Correct paper shows (a) the vector cross product p×E evaluated component-wise to give τ with numerical components and units N·m (for example τ = ... î + ... ĵ + ... k̂ N·m), and (b) a statement 'net force = 0' with a brief reason that forces on the two point charges cancel in a uniform field and the unit of force given as N.

homework.submission_format: Show calculations on paper or a single PDF containing work, with units on every line; label final answers clearly.
tasks: Compute the torque (vector and magnitude) for three dipoles: (i) p = 1.5 î C·m in E = 2.0 ĵ N/C, (ii) p = 2.0(î+ĵ) C·m in E = 1.0(î−ĵ) N/C, (iii) p = 0.8 ĵ C·m in E = 0.50 k̂ N/C. Write units explicitly and show cross-product work. (Estimated time: 15 min)

Using the far-field axis formula E_axis = (1/4πε0)(2p/r^3), compute the magnitude of the electric field on-axis for a dipole with p = 6.0×10−6 C·m at (a) r = 0.50 m and (b) r = 1.0 m. Use ε0 = 8.85×10−12 C^2/(N·m^2). Carry units through each step and compare the ratio E(0.5)/E(1.0). (Estimated time: 20 min)

Short explanation (one paragraph): Why does the dipole far-field go like 1/r^3 instead of 1/r^2? Anchor your answer to the physical picture of two opposite charges separated by 2a and mention what happens as r ≫ a. (Estimated time: 10 min)

mentor_moment.story: In my lab a tiny charged bead kept rotating on a pivot until I realised the bead and its opposite partner made a dipole: the pivot didn't move because the net force was zero, but the pair kept turning until p aligned with E.
mentor_moment.takeaway: If a system rotates but its center doesn't move, check torque (N·m); if the center translates, check net force (N).
mentor_moment.title: The lab clamp that taught torque

anticipated_questions: Why is dipole moment p defined as q times distance and not q times 2a? (Answer: p uses the vector from − to +; with symmetric charges separated by 2a, magnitude p = q·(2a).)
What are the units of flux? (Answer: N·m^2/C or V·m depending on route.)
Is p a vector? (Answer: Yes, direction from negative to positive charge.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write short reminders and units.
teacher_script.heading: Warm-up recall and check entry ticket
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Collect one-line answers quickly: "Who circled 1/r^3? Who circled 1/r^2?" Pause for 3 quick hands. Read one student reason for 1/r^2 if present. Then say: "We recall three things before we start: (1) Coulomb's law gives force and field units, (2) dipole moment p = q·(2a/2?) — no: we defined p as q times vector from − to + with units coulomb·metre (C·m), and (3) electric flux idea and units. I'll write these on the board now and we will use them with units in every step." If a student says 'I guessed 1/r^2', ask: "What cancellation did you imagine?" and note the answer briefly.

anticipated_questions: Why do 1/r^2 terms cancel? (Answer: because the charges are equal and opposite; their leading-order fields at large r are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign along that direction.)
How do you get binomial expansion? (Answer: show 1/(r±a)^2 ≈ 1/r^2 · (1 ∓ 2a/r + ...), can accept result without full derivation if pressed.)
Why is qa replaced by p/2? (Answer: because p = q·(2a), so qa = p/2.)
Are the directions always exactly along or opposite p? (Answer: on axis yes; equatorial yes for r≫a approximation.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the step-by-step algebra for axis and equatorial expansions, keeping units on key terms.
teacher_script.heading: Derive far-field dipole E ~ 1/r^3 (axis and equatorial)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We will do a step-by-step derivation for points on the dipole axis and on the equatorial plane. Keep units at every line. Take charges +q at x=+a and −q at x=−a on x-axis. Point P is at distance r from origin with r ≫ a. Start with Coulomb's law for a point charge: E = (1/(4πε0))·q/r'^2 in N/C. First, axis case: P on +x axis at x=r. Distances: r+ = r−a and r− = r+a. Write their magnitudes to first non-zero order using binomial expansion: 1/(r±a)^2 ≈ 1/r^2 · (1 ∓ 2a/r + 3( a^2 / r^2) ...). Show subtraction of contributions from +q and −q and keep leading nonzero term. Explain cancellation of 1/r^2 terms and that the leading term in E_x is proportional to qa/r^3. Replace qa by p/2? Wait: clarify magnitude: with charges ±q separated by 2a, the dipole moment magnitude p = q·(2a). So qa = p/2. Substitute to get E_axis = (1/(4πε0))·2p / r^3 in direction of p. Do this slowly, writing units: q in C, a in m so p in C·m, 1/(4πε0) in N·m^2/C^2, r^3 in m^3 so overall N/C. Repeat for equatorial point at y=r (perp) where contributions add with opposite sign to axis case and show E_equatorial = −(1/(4πε0))·p / r^3 (pointing opposite to p). Emphasize the signs: axis points along p, equatorial points opposite p. At each algebra step say the units and simplify to N/C."

anticipated_questions: Is the external field really uniform? (Answer: approximately uniform between large plates; discuss limits.)
What if the dipole were free to move? (Answer: it would both experience torque and possibly net force if field non-uniform.)
How accurate is the fall-off demonstration? (Answer: qualitative; we will rely on algebraic derivation for exact power law.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write measured values, compute p numerically with units, compute τ = pE sinθ with numeric result and units.
teacher_script.heading: Demonstration: torque and fall-off
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Set up two small charged spheres on a rotatable jig showing a pair ±q separated by 2a. Apply a uniform external E (from two large parallel plates) to show a torque. Say: "Observe rotation: the dipole aligns with E. Measure and call out values: q = 2.0×10−6 C (if using values), separation 2a = 4.0 cm, so p = q·(2a) = 2.0×10−6 C × 0.04 m = 8.0×10−8 C·m. External field E measured as 2000 N/C (or 2.0×10^3 N/C). Compute torque magnitude τ = pE sinθ and units N·m right here on the board with numbers. Pick one angle θ = 30° to calculate a number. Then move the detector probe along the axis away from the dipole and show field decreasing faster than 1/r^2 (qualitatively) — students note distances (m) and relative readings (N/C). Ask students to write down the measured quantities and units in their notebooks."

anticipated_questions: Can we use k = 8.99×10^9 instead of 1/(4πε0)? (Answer: yes; it's the same constant with units N·m^2/C^2.)
Why does τ have units N·m? (Answer: because p (C·m) times E (N/C) gives N·m.)
Why use r≫a? (Answer: the far-field formulas assume r much larger than the charge separation so higher-order terms are negligible.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write both practice problems and then solve (A) with numeric steps and units; keep (B) available for pairs to use and for teacher to complete if asked.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice: compute torque and dipole field numbers
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Put students in pairs. Hand out two short problems on the board: (A) Given p = 6.0×10−7 C·m and uniform E = 1.5×10^3 N/C at angle 45°, compute τ magnitude and units. (B) Given a dipole with p = 1.0×10−6 C·m, compute the magnitude of E on the axis at r = 0.50 m using E_axis formula with ε0 = 8.85×10−12 C^2/(N·m^2). Work the first problem together on the board step by step, showing units. Then send pairs to work on B; circulate, prompt students to substitute p and r into the formula E_axis = (1/(4πε0))·2p/r^3 and check units result N/C. If students get stuck, show algebra of plugging numbers into 1/(4πε0) ≈ 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. Encourage unit cancellation: (N·m^2/C^2)·(C·m)/m^3 = N/C."

anticipated_questions: Why no net force in uniform E? (Answer: forces on +q and −q are equal and opposite so they sum to zero.)
What if the field is not uniform? (Answer: then net force can be nonzero; we only say zero for ideal uniform E.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the two questions and the expected short answers after collecting responses.
teacher_script.heading: Formative check (two quick questions)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Hand out or display two short written questions: 1) "State: does an ideal dipole in a uniform external electric field experience a net force? Give a one-sentence explanation and state units of the torque and force." 2) "If the dipole field at r1 is E1, what is the ratio E(r1)/E(r2) for r2 = 2·r1 using the far-field 1/r^3 law? Show calculation." Give 2 minutes for answers, collect, mark quickly: for Q1 expect 'no net force; torque may exist; force units N; torque units N·m.' For Q2 expect ratio 8. Give immediate verbal feedback and correct common errors.

anticipated_questions: Do we need to memorize signs for axis vs equatorial? (Answer: yes—axis is +2p/r^3 along p; equatorial is −p/r^3 opposite p.)
Will we use Gauss's law next? (Answer: yes, for continuous charge distributions like wires and planes.)
teacher_script.board_action: Box the final formulas and write the homework reference (page and problem numbers).
teacher_script.heading: Consolidation and homework
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Read aloud the final boxed formulas on the board and point to units: "These are the far-field dipole formulas and Gauss's law you'll need next. For homework: problems connecting dipole far-field approximations to Gauss-law problems (fields of wires, planes, shells preview)." Remind students to copy formulas and unit-check all answers.

bullet_points: Gauss's law: flux through closed surface = Q_enclosed / ε0
ε0 units appear so E has units N/C; carry units through every step
surface charge density σ = dQ/dS (units C/m^2)
linear charge density λ = dQ/dl (units C/m)
volume charge density ρ = dQ/dV (units C/m^3)
For an infinite plane: choose pillbox, dQ = σ A ⇒ 2 E A = σ A / ε0 ⇒ E = σ/(2 ε0) (N/C), normal to plane
For an infinite line: choose coaxial cylinder, Q_enclosed = λ L ⇒ E (2π r L) = λ L / ε0 ⇒ E = λ/(2π ε0 r) (N/C), radial
For a thin spherical shell: outside E (4π r^2) = q/ε0 ⇒ E = q/(4π ε0 r^2) (N/C); inside E = 0
Common errors: missing factor 2 for plane, missing 2π for wire, forgetting units
diagrams_to_draw: Point charge at center of a sphere (label q and radius r)
Infinite plane with pillbox straddling plane (label area A and arrows for E above and below)
Infinite wire with coaxial cylinder (label λ, radius r, length L)
Thin spherical shell with two Gaussian surfaces: r>R and r<R (label q and R)

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Flux = ∮E·dA = E·A (top) + E·A (bottom) = 2EA. Enclosed charge Qenc = σ·A (units C). Gauss's law: 2EA = Qenc/ε0 = σA/ε0. Cancel A: E = σ/(2ε0). Units: σ is C/m^2, ε0 is C^2/(N·m^2) so E in N/C.
checkpoint_questions.question: You place a Gaussian pillbox that straddles an infinite charged plane with surface charge density σ. Write the flux integral and show the algebraic steps that lead to the field magnitude E on one side of the plane. (Answer in symbols, carry units.)

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Symmetry: E is radial and constant on curved surface, and zero on the flat end faces because E is perpendicular to their normals. Flux = E·(curved area) = E(2πrL). Qenc = λL. Gauss's law: E(2πrL) = λL/ε0 ⇒ E = λ/(2π ε0 r). Units: λ is C/m so E in N/C.
checkpoint_questions.question: For an infinitely long straight wire with linear density λ, you choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L. Write the steps to get E(r). Explain why the curved side contributes and the ends do or do not.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Outside (r > R): E = q/(4π ε0 r^2) radial (N/C). Inside (r < R): E = 0 (N/C). Reason: For a Gaussian sphere of radius r < R no charge is enclosed (Qenc = 0) so ∮E·dA = 0 ⇒ E = 0 by symmetry.
checkpoint_questions.question: State the electric field produced by a uniformly charged thin spherical shell at a point r inside the shell (r < R) and at a point outside (r > R). Give a one-sentence reason, using Gauss's law, for the inside result.

entry_ticket.prompt: Write a one-line answer (magnitude and direction) to this: A uniformly charged thin spherical shell carries total charge q. What is the electric field at the exact centre of the shell? Give a number or expression and a direction. No explanation needed.

exit_ticket.prompt: A large metal plate has σ = 10.0 μC/m^2. A long thin wire parallel to the plate carries λ = 5.0 nC/m and is located 2.0 cm from the plate. Treat the plate as an infinite plane and the wire as an infinite line. Using superposition, write expressions (with units) for the magnitudes of the electric fields from the plate and from the wire at the point halfway between them (1.0 cm from the plate). Then state the net field direction assuming the plate is positively charged and the wire is positively charged.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Student writes E_plate = σ/(2ε0) with σ = 10.0×10^-6 C/m^2 giving numerical N/C; E_wire = λ/(2π ε0 r) with λ = 5.0×10^-9 C/m and r = 0.01 m giving numerical N/C; then states net field magnitude as vector sum of magnitudes with directions: plate field points away from plate, wire field points radially away from wire, and specifies the resulting direction at the midway point.

homework.submission_format: handwritten scan or photo (one page) showing all steps and units
tasks: Calculate the electric field magnitude and direction 2.0 cm from an infinite wire with λ = 5.0 nC/m. Show all steps, include units at each line, and give a numeric answer in N/C.
A uniformly charged infinite plane has σ = 10 μC/m^2. Find the electric field 1.0 mm from the plane. Show units through the algebra and give the numeric N/C value.

A thin spherical shell has total charge q = 2.0 μC and radius R = 5.0 cm. (a) Compute E at r = 3.0 cm (inside) and r = 10.0 cm (outside). Show Gauss's law steps and units, and give numeric answers in N/C.

mentor_moment.story: In a demo, a charged metal plate made hair stand on end for students nearby. They expected the field to drop with distance but hair reacted even a few centimetres away because a charged plate's field stays nearly constant close to it.
mentor_moment.takeaway: For a large charged plate the field near it is roughly constant and equals σ/(2ε0), so moving a short distance doesn't change the field much.
mentor_moment.title: The Van de Graaff Plate Surprise

anticipated_questions: Why do we carry N/C rather than N? (Because E is force per unit charge.)
Do we always get E by dividing Q by ε0? (Only for suitable symmetry or after computing flux.)
Why use a sphere here? (Because symmetry makes E constant on the spherical surface.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write Gauss's law sentence. Underline ε0 and write units. Draw a small point charge at center of a sphere and label q, r. Write the quick derivation: flux = E·4πr^2 = q/ε0 ⇒ E = q/(4πε0 r^2).
teacher_script.heading: Quick Gauss review & units (activate prior knowledge)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Hold up the sheet titled “Gauss’s law” and read it exactly: “Electric flux through a closed surface = Q_enclosed / ε0.” Point to ε0 and say: “ε0 is a constant; its units are C^2/(N·m^2) so the right side has units C/(C^2/(N·m^2)) = N·m^2/C·m = N·m/C. But flux has units E·area, so E must end up in N/C. We will carry units C, m, N/C in every step.” Ask: “What is the flux through a closed surface that encloses a single point charge q?” Wait for reply. Then write the point-charge example quickly: use Coulomb’s law for a point charge at center of spherical surface to show how flux = E(4πr^2) = q/ε0 and therefore E = q/(4πε0 r^2) (we will derive spherical shell formally later).

anticipated_questions: Why is there a 2? (Because flux passes through both faces of the pillbox.)
What if the plane is a conductor? (Charge sits on surface; outside field is same form but inside conductor E=0.)
How large must a real plate be for 'infinite' to hold? (Enough so edge effects are negligible at the point of interest.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw plane and pillbox. Write definition: σ = dQ/dS (units C/m^2). Write dQ = σ A. Write flux = 2 E A. Write Gauss: 2 E A = σ A / ε0 ⇒ E = σ/(2 ε0). Note units N/C beside final line.
teacher_script.heading: Derive field of infinite plane (Gaussian pillbox)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: “We now use Gauss’s law to find E near an infinite flat sheet with uniform surface charge density sigma (σ). Definition: σ = dQ/dS with units C/m^2.” Draw one infinite plane as a horizontal line and place a small pillbox straddling it. Verbally: “Choose a short cylindrical pillbox whose flat faces are equal area A, one face above the plane and one below. The curved side contributes no flux because E is perpendicular to the plane by symmetry.” Ask: “What is dQ in terms of σ and A?” Pause for reply; then state and write: dQ = σ A (units C). Now compute flux: flux = E·A (top) + E·A (bottom) = 2EA because E has same magnitude on both sides and points away from the sheet. Apply Gauss’s law: 2 E A = Q_enclosed/ε0 = σ A/ε0. Cancel A and solve for E = σ/(2 ε0). Say units explicitly: σ (C/m^2) divided by ε0 (C^2/(N·m^2)) gives N/C. Point to a physical example: a charged metal plate; remind that result assumes infinite sheet or near center of a very large sheet.”

anticipated_questions: Why ignore the flat ends? (E is parallel to end faces by symmetry, so no flux there.)
What if wire is not infinite? (Near an end, symmetry breaks and formula no longer exact.)
Why does E drop as 1/r not 1/r^2? (Because the Gaussian surface area grows linearly with r for a cylinder.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw wire and cylindrical surface. Write definition λ = dQ/dl (C/m). Write Q_enclosed = λ L. Write flux = E (2π r L). Write Gauss: E (2π r L) = λ L / ε0 ⇒ E = λ/(2π ε0 r). Add direction: radial (ˆr). Add units N/C.
teacher_script.heading: Derive field of infinite line (cylindrical Gaussian surface)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: “Now consider an infinitely long straight wire with linear charge density λ. Definition: λ = dQ/dl with units C/m.” Draw a long vertical wire and coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L. Ask: “What is the enclosed charge Q_enclosed for that cylinder?” Wait briefly, then write: Q_enclosed = λ L (units C). Explain symmetry: E must point radially outward and be constant on the curved surface. The flat ends give no flux because E is parallel to them. Compute flux through curved surface: flux = E (2π r L). Apply Gauss's law: E (2π r L) = λ L / ε0. Cancel L and solve: E = λ/(2π ε0 r). Explicitly carry units: λ (C/m) divided by ε0 (C^2/(N·m^2)) and r (m) gives N/C. Emphasize direction: radially outward (draw arrow). Mention physical example: thin charged wire.

anticipated_questions: Why is the inside field zero? (Because no charge is enclosed by a Gaussian surface inside the shell.)
Is the shell result exact for any shell thickness? (We used a thin shell; a uniformly filled sphere has a different inside E.)
Does the result depend on how charge is distributed on the shell surface? (If distribution is uniform it holds; asymmetric distribution breaks symmetry.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw spherical shell, label radius R and total q (C). Draw two Gaussian radii r>R and r<R. Write flux outside: E (4π r^2) = q/ε0 ⇒ E = q/(4π ε0 r^2) (N/C). Write inside: Q_enclosed = 0 ⇒ E = 0.
teacher_script.heading: Derive field of thin spherical shell (inside and outside)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: “Finally, a uniformly charged thin spherical shell with total charge q. Use spherical Gaussian surfaces centered on the shell.” Draw sphere and two Gaussian radii: one r > R (outside) and one r < R (inside). State: “The shell’s total charge is q (units C). For r > R by symmetry E is radial and constant on a spherical surface of radius r. Enclosed charge = q. Flux = E (4π r^2). Gauss: E (4π r^2) = q/ε0 ⇒ E = q/(4π ε0 r^2), directed radially outward.” Write units N/C. Then r < R: “For a Gaussian surface inside the hollow shell the enclosed charge is zero, Q_enclosed = 0, so E = 0.” Ask students to compare this outside formula to the point-charge result we recalled at the start and confirm they are identical. Emphasize physical meaning: outside the shell it behaves exactly like a point charge at center; inside there is no field from the shell charges.

anticipated_questions: How do I convert nC/m to C/m? (Multiply nC by 1e-9; 5 nC/m = 5×10^-9 C/m.)
For the plane, why doesn't r appear in the answer? (Because E for infinite plane is independent of distance.)
When plugging numbers, what value of ε0 do we use? (ε0 = 8.85×10^-12 C^2/(N·m^2); carry units through.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the three practice problems clearly with given numbers: (a) λ = 5 nC/m, r = 2.0 cm. (b) σ = 10 μC/m^2, distance 1.0 mm. (c) q = 2.0 μC, r = 0.5R and r = 2.0R. Remind: show units at each step.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice (teacher-led calculations in pairs)
teacher_script.speaker_notes:
Hand out a worksheet with three short calculations. Read each aloud and have students work in pairs while you circulate and prompt them to write units at every step.
Problem (a): “An infinite wire has λ = 5 nC/m. Find E at r = 2.0 cm. Show units.” (Expect use E = λ/(2π ε0 r).) 
Problem (b): “An infinite plane has σ = 10 μC/m^2. Find E at 1.0 mm from the plane. Show units and direction.” (Expect E = σ/(2 ε0).) 
Problem (c): “A thin spherical shell has q = 2.0 μC. Find E at r = 0.5 R and at r = 2.0 R. Show units.” (Expect E_inside = 0 and E_outside = q/(4π ε0 r^2).)
Ask pairs to write final answers with numeric substitution and N/C units. Tell them you will collect one answer sheet for quick checking.

anticipated_questions: Will we need these formulas on the test? (Yes, for symmetric charge problems.)
What if charges are not uniform? (Then Gauss's law still holds but symmetry may not let you solve for E easily.)
How strict is the infinite assumption? (Infinite is idealized; large compared to observation distance is the practical requirement.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write three consolidation questions for students to copy. Underline common errors: factor of 2, factor of 2π, units. Re-list final takeaway formulas (as written below).
teacher_script.heading: Check & consolidate (quick quiz and summary)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Project three very short questions and ask students to write answers on a slip: (1) Give σ, λ, ρ definitions with units. (2) True/False: Field outside a thin spherical shell equals field of a point charge at the center. (3) For an infinite line, how does E scale with r? Collect slips quickly. Then say aloud the common errors: forgetting factors of 2 for the plane, dropping 2π for the wire, forgetting to include units. Finish with the three takeaways: definitions of densities, the three field formulas we derived, and always track units. Dismiss.

prerequisites.statement: Familiarity with vector notation including unit vectors and vector addition as used in force and field expressions.
Basic algebra and ability to manipulate inverse-square relations.

diagnostic_questions.question: Two identical point charges separated by 1.0 m repel with force F. If the separation is increased to 2.0 m, what is the new magnitude of the force?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student recognises the inverse-square dependence (correct: F/4) or instead applies an inverse-linear rule (wrong: F/2).

diagnostic_questions.question: Two point charges separated by 3.0 m have force F between them. If the separation is reduced to 1.0 m, what is the new force?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student computes the factor (3^2 = 9 → force increases by 9) or uses linear scaling (factor of 3). A linear answer shows they are treating dependence as inverse-linear, not inverse-square.

learning_gaps.misconception: If I double the distance between two charges, the electrostatic force becomes half of what it was.

remediation.action: Begin with a hands-on lab: measure electrostatic force (or use a Coulomb-force simulation) for one fixed pair of point-like charges at separations 1.0 m, 2.0 m and 3.0 m. Have students record the numerical forces and compute the ratios F(1m)/F(2m) and F(1m)/F(3m).
remediation.rationale: Concrete measurements force students to confront the actual numeric change. Seeing ratios near 4 and 9 (not 2 and 3) ties the exponent to measurable outcomes and breaks the habit of linear scaling.

remediation.action: Guide a derivation on the board: start from the statement 'force ∝ 1/r^2', substitute r→2r and r→3r, and carry units and algebra through to show F becomes F/4 and F/9. Ask students to explain each algebraic step in plain language (e.g. 'squaring the distance doubles squaring effect').
remediation.rationale: Deriving the numerical factor step-by-step links the algebraic form to the numeric change; requiring them to paraphrase prevents memorised symbol manipulation and shows why the exponent matters, not just the word 'inverse'.

remediation.action: Use contrasting examples: compare three laws (inverse, inverse-square, inverse-cube) on a table with sample r values (1,2,3) and computed factors, and ask students to predict which physical situations match each law (e.g. springs ~ linear, gravity/electrostatics ~ inverse-square). Follow with a short quiz question that asks for the factor when r is scaled by arbitrary k.
remediation.rationale: Placing inverse-square alongside other dependences highlights the qualitative difference produced by changing the exponent. Connecting to other physical systems provides a source of correct generalisation and helps students replace the incorrect rule-of-thumb with a discriminating strategy for interpreting 'varies as'.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: Zero — because the charges add to zero so there can't be a field.
diagnostic_questions.question: Two point charges, +Q and −Q, are fixed a short distance d apart (a dipole). At a point along the line perpendicular to the midpoint and at distance R (with R >> d), is there an electric field? If so, is it zero, and what direction does it point?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If a student answers 'zero' this reveals they believe net charge alone determines whether a field exists and are not applying vector superposition to spatially separated charges.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: No — the rod is neutral overall so it produces no electric field and the test charge won't feel a force.
diagnostic_questions.question: A neutral insulating rod has +Q concentrated near one end and −Q concentrated near the other. A small positive test charge is brought near the +Q end. Will the test charge feel a force? If yes, in which direction?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If a student says 'no force', it shows they think neutrality eliminates local fields and forces, ignoring local nonzero fields from charge separation.

learning_gaps.misconception: If the total charge of an object or system is zero, it produces no electric field anywhere (so neutral means no field).

remediation.action: Start with a live or simulated demonstration: place two equal and opposite point charges separated by a small distance. Use an electric field sensor, a compass-like field indicator, or a field-line simulation to map the field at several nearby points and at a point far away. Record vector directions and magnitudes and display numeric sensor readings with units (N/C).
remediation.rationale: Seeing nonzero, directional field readings despite net zero charge confronts the overgeneralisation from neutrality. Explicit numeric vector measurements force students to treat field as a vector sum of contributions from each charge (not a single-scalar property of 'net charge'). Carrying units (N/C) ties the abstract to measurable force per unit test charge.

remediation.action: Derive the field of the dipole on the board step-by-step: write the expression for the field from each point charge (showing magnitudes and directions with units), expand for R >> d to show the leading-order nonzero term, and compare the 1/r dependence of a single charge vs. the faster fall-off for the dipole. Keep units through every line and compute a numerical example (choose Q, d, R) so students calculate concrete N/C values.
remediation.rationale: A careful algebraic superposition shows cancellation is partial, not complete, and the derivation anchors the result in the same arithmetic students use in other problems. The numerical example connects the symbolic expansion to measurable magnitudes so students stop treating 'zero net charge' as a rule and instead see how geometry controls the field.

remediation.action: Give a short guided worksheet: several quick tasks where students must predict field direction and relative magnitude (then check with simulation/sensor): (a) two like charges, (b) two opposite charges separated, (c) neutral distribution with separated clusters. Each task asks them to compute vector sums for at least two points and to explain in one sentence why 'net charge = 0' does or does not imply zero field at that point.
remediation.rationale: Active calculation and explanation forces students to practise vector addition and to articulate the specific failure of the misconception (distribution matters). Having them compare prediction with measurement/simulation gives immediate feedback that contradicts the false generalisation, and the explanation step promotes conceptual change rather than memorising a correction.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: The +3 μC at 0.30 m reduces the force from the +2 μC at 0 m on the +1 μC, so you should 'scale down' that pairwise force. The net force is much smaller than the simple vector sum — about half the value you'd get if you just added pairwise forces.
diagnostic_questions.question: Three point charges lie on a line: a +2 μC at x = 0 m, a +1 μC at x = 0.10 m, and a +3 μC at x = 0.30 m. What is the force on the +1 μC charge? (A student who holds the misconception will answer incorrectly.)
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If the student changes the computed force between +1 μC and one neighbour because of the presence of the other, they do not apply superposition correctly.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: The force will not be F1+F2; because the charges interact among themselves the individual forces change, so the net will be some different value (not the sum), maybe less because of mutual influence.
diagnostic_questions.question: You measure the force on a small test charge q0 when only charge Q1 is present and get F1. Then you remove Q1 and instead put only Q2 in the same place where Q1 had been and measure force F2. Now you put both Q1 and Q2 together; what do you expect the force on q0 to be?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: A wrong answer shows the student thinks the presence of the second charge changes the pairwise interaction between the first and the test charge (not simply that two forces exist and sum).

learning_gaps.misconception: If there are several charges near a test charge, each charge's force on the test charge is different from what it would be if the other charges weren't there — so you have to 'adjust' each pairwise force to account for the others.

remediation.action: Lab or live demo: use a Coulomb-force sensor or high-quality simulation. Place a test charge q0 on a force sensor and measure the force when only Q1 is present; record magnitude and direction with units (N). Remove Q1 and measure force with only Q2 present. Finally place Q1 and Q2 together and measure the force on q0. Have students compute the vector sum F1 + F2 (show units N) before revealing the measured combined force.
remediation.rationale: Concrete measurement ties the abstract statement to physical evidence and units. Seeing that the measured combined force equals the arithmetic vector sum of the two previously measured forces shows that the presence of another charge does not alter the individual pairwise forces on the test charge.

remediation.action: Derivation and guided worksheet: derive the force on a test charge from Coulomb's law for two source charges by writing the forces from each source explicitly as vectors (showing magnitudes in N and unit vectors), then add them algebraically to get the total. Emphasise step-by-step where linearity enters (no cross-terms). Then repeat the algebra including an extra charge to show the pattern generalises.
remediation.rationale: A stepwise derivation makes it clear that Coulomb's law gives independent pairwise forces that sum; showing units (N) and unit vectors prevents hiding the vector nature. Demonstrating there are no terms that multiply charges together beyond pairwise products addresses the mistaken idea that charges 'modify' other pairwise forces.

remediation.action: Conceptual question sequence and analogy: ask students to consider gravitational forces between small masses as a close analogy — have them calculate the gravitational force on a small mass due to two separated masses by summing vectors, then discuss why adding a third object doesn't change the force between any specific pair. Follow with targeted questions: 'If Q2 is far away, does it change the Coulomb force between Q1 and q0?' and ask for justification referring to the measurements and algebra.
remediation.rationale: Analogies to familiar inverse-square forces where superposition holds help students transfer correct intuition. The guided questions force explicit reasoning about independence of pairwise interactions rather than vague appeals to 'influence' or 'shielding.'

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: No — there's no field there unless I put a test charge there. Only when I put a test charge will a force appear, so the field depends on which test charge I use.
diagnostic_questions.question: You remove every charged object except one point charge +Q fixed in space. At a location 10 cm from +Q there is no test charge present. Is there an electric field at that location? Explain and, if yes, state how its magnitude depends on anything you place there later.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student thinks the field is only present when a test charge is placed there, or whether they understand the field exists independently. A wrong answer shows they conflate force measurement with existence of the field.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: F2 will be different and also the electric field will be different when I use a bigger test charge — the field becomes three times larger with q2 because the field depends on the charge I use to probe it.
diagnostic_questions.question: A point charge +Q is fixed. You first place a small test charge +q1 at a point and measure a force F1; later you replace it with a different test charge +q2 and measure force F2. If q2 = 3 q1, what should you expect for F2 and for the electric field magnitude E at that point in the two trials?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student recognises that force changes proportionally with test charge while the field (F/q) stays the same. A wrong answer shows they believe the field itself changes with the test charge.

learning_gaps.misconception: There is no electric field at a point until I put a test charge there, and the field depends on which test charge I use (its size or sign).

remediation.action: Derive E = F/q at the board starting from Coulomb's law: write F = k Q q / r^2, then divide both sides by q to get E = k Q / r^2. Work the algebra symbolically and then plug in two different numerical q values to show E is unchanged.
remediation.rationale: Algebraically cancelling q directly addresses the source of the mistake (confusion from the product form of Coulomb's law). Showing the same E with different numerical q makes explicit that the probe's charge drops out and that E depends only on source charges and geometry.

remediation.action: Class experiment or computer simulation: fix a source charge Q and measure the force on two different test charges (one positive small q1, one larger q2, and one negative -q3). Students compute E = F/q for each trial and record the values.
remediation.rationale: Hands-on measurement ties the abstract quantity E to measurable numbers while revealing the pattern: forces change with q but the quotient F/q stays the same (and flips sign appropriately for negative q). This confronts the 'nothing exists until probed' intuition by showing consistent E values even when different probes are used.

remediation.action: Show a field-line diagram or a vector-field plot for the same source charge with no test charge drawn. Ask students to sketch or describe what a small positive and a small negative test charge placed at a point would do, predicting directions and relative magnitudes, then compare to E = kQ/r^2.
remediation.rationale: Separates the visual model of a field (arrows in space) from specific probes and reinforces that the field is a property of space around sources. Asking students to predict probe behaviour from that field challenges the reverse inference (that probes create the field).

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: Yes — rubbing created extra negative charge on the rod (and a positive charge on the sweater), so the total amount of charge in the system has increased; it is no longer zero.
diagnostic_questions.question: You rub a plastic rod on your wool sweater. Before rubbing, the rod and sweater together had zero net charge. After rubbing, the rod is negatively charged and the sweater is positively charged. Has the total electric charge of the rod+sweater system changed? Explain.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student believes rubbing created net charge rather than transferring it between bodies.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: The net charge inside the box has increased (there is now extra charge produced by the rubbing), so the box has a net non-zero charge.
diagnostic_questions.question: You take an isolated box containing two neutral objects. You rub them together inside the closed box. After rubbing, you measure each object and find one is negative and the other positive. What is the net charge inside the box now, and why?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If the student insists that rubbing makes new charge appear inside an isolated system (violating conservation) instead of recognising equal and opposite transfer.

evidence.quote: No new charge is created in the process of rubbing.

learning_gaps.misconception: Rubbing two objects creates new electric charge — when I rub a rod on fur (or two materials together) I make charge out of nothing so the total amount of charge in the system increases.

remediation.action: Token-transfer activity (10 minutes): Give each pair of students a set of small identical tokens labelled 'electron' and two cardboard cut-outs representing Material A and Material B. Start both materials neutral (same number of electron tokens). Have students physically move a small, fixed number of electron tokens from A to B to model rubbing, then count tokens on each.
remediation.rationale: A concrete particle model makes 'transfer' visible: students see no tokens are created or destroyed, only moved. This addresses the root overgeneralisation by showing how local charging arises from redistribution of discrete charges.

remediation.action: Quantitative classroom demo with an electroscope or simple Faraday-cup setup (15 minutes): Show the electroscope reading when two neutral metal cans are connected (zero). Rub a plastic rod on fur to charge it, touch the rod to one can (observe electroscope change), then touch the two cans together and show the combined reading equals the algebraic sum of earlier readings (or that the net charge of the closed system before and after remains the same). If available, use an electrometer to measure total charge before and after rubbing two objects inside an isolated container.
remediation.rationale: A measured, repeatable experiment ties the abstract conservation law to numbers and instrument readings. Seeing that instrument readings add algebraically (and that the total measured charge of an isolated system stays constant) corrects the intuition that rubbing 'creates' charge.

remediation.action: Guided questioning and atomic picture (8 minutes): Lead students through a short sequence: (a) Ask what a material's neutral state means in terms of electrons/protons; (b) Ask where extra negative charge on a rubbed object comes from (answer: electrons moved from the other object); (c) Ask what must happen to the other object's charge when electrons leave. Use unit notation (charge in coulombs) for an example transfer (e.g. −3.2×10−19 C corresponds to one electron) to show discrete transfers and conservation.
remediation.rationale: Explicitly connecting macroscopic observations to the microscopic electron-transfer model and carrying units/quantities enforces that charge is quantised and conserved. Using a specific numerical example prevents hand-waving and helps students replace 'creation' language with 'transfer of discrete charges.'

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: The charge stays right where the rod touched the sphere; it doesn't move around.
diagnostic_questions.question: You touch a charged rod to one point on a metal (conducting) sphere and then remove the rod. Where is the net charge located on the sphere after you remove the rod?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If the student says the charge remains only at the point where the rod touched, they still believe charge is immobile on conductors and have not grasped free electron redistribution.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: The charge stays only at the rubbed patch in both the plastic ruler and the metal spoon; it doesn't spread out on the spoon either.
diagnostic_questions.question: You charge a small patch on a plastic ruler by rubbing it with a cloth. Then you do the same rubbing to one patch on a metal spoon (both isolated on insulating stands). After removing the cloth, in which case does the charge stay only at the rubbed patch and in which case does it spread out?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If the student says the charge stays localized on both the ruler and the spoon, they are overgeneralising the insulator behaviour to conductors and haven't learned that conductors let charge move to the surface.

evidence.quote: When some charge is transferred to a conductor, it readily gets distributed over the entire surface of the conductor. In contrast, if some charge is put on an insulator, it stays at the same place.

learning_gaps.misconception: Electric charge placed on any material always stays where it is put and does not move.

remediation.action: Prediction prompt: Ask students to predict what will happen when a charged metal sphere A is touched to an identical neutral metal sphere B (both on insulating stands). Record predictions. Then perform the classic experiment: charge sphere A (by rubbing or using an electroscope), touch A to B briefly, separate them, and measure the charge on each with an electroscope or by observing attraction to small bits of paper.
remediation.rationale: Making predictions forces commitment to the erroneous rule and makes the subsequent observable contradiction meaningful. Demonstrating that both spheres share/redistribute the charge provides direct, measurable evidence that charge moves across conductors rather than staying where placed.

remediation.action: Faraday pail or metal-can demo: Place a charged conductor inside a metal pail connected to an electroscope (or use a metal can as a conductor). Show that the electroscope registers the same net charge regardless of where the charge is placed on the inner object; then touch the inside and outside to show charge resides on the outer surface of the conductor.
remediation.rationale: This ties the abstract rule (free charges move to the surface of a conductor) to a macroscopic measurement. Students observe that charge redistributes to the conductor's surface and that internal points do not retain isolated charge, countering the 'charge stays where put' generalisation.

remediation.action: Direct contrast activity: Have pairs of students charge a small plastic strip and a small metal strip in identical ways. Let them mark the rubbed spot and then probe different locations (with electroscope, tiny pith balls, or by measuring attraction of small paper) to map where the charge effects occur on each material. Students then compare results and explain differences.
remediation.rationale: Confronting the two materials side-by-side links the observed difference to the cause named in the misconception: material-dependent electron mobility. Students see the localized effect on the insulator and the redistributed effect on the conductor and must reconcile their prior overgeneralisation with this evidence.

periods.sequence_rationale: As the opening period, this lesson introduces the two kinds of electric charge, everyday static-electricity examples, and conductor/insulator behaviour; it builds the concrete ideas and measurement conventions needed to derive and apply Coulomb's law and supports the next period on Quantisation of charge, Coulomb's law, and Principle of superposition.

time_allocation.label: Activate prior knowledge with demonstrations of everyday static electricity (sparks, charged plastic, hair standing); ask students to describe observed forces and record qualitative direction and magnitude impressions in words and simple sketches (anchor in volts/charge verbally)

Introduce the concept of two kinds of charge and conductor vs insulator: define 'charge' with units coulomb (C), show small charged pith-ball/commercial electroscope demo and explain charge redistribution on conductors vs fixed charge on insulators

Derive Coulomb's law step by step from an experimental setup: explain point-charge idealisation, present empirical 1/r^2 dependence from two-charge experiment, introduce constant k and write magnitude form F = k|q1 q2|/r^2 with units (N), and show vector direction rule (repel/attract) tied to sign

Guided practice: pairs calculate magnitude and direction of force for two given point charges (explicit numbers, carry units through: q1 in C, q2 in C, r in m → F in N), teacher circulates and checks unit algebra and vector direction

Check understanding and consolidate: short written diagnostic (2 problems: sign/direction and a units check) followed by whole-class discussion linking results to next period's focus on charge quantisation and superposition

periods.title: Charges, Conductors, and Coulomb Force

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds on 'Charges, Conductors, and Coulomb Force' by formalising charge as quantised (multiples of e) and deriving Coulomb's inverse-square force law and the superposition rule; it prepares students to use point-source forces to define the 'Electric field' and to analyse test/source charge setups in the following period.

time_allocation.label: Activate prior knowledge: rapid warm-up recalling conductors/insulators, +/− charge examples, and one schematic of two point charges from the previous lesson (students state expected force direction)

Introduce quantisation of charge: stepwise explanation linking atoms, electrons (charge −e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C) and protons, show conservation in an isolated system using a simple electron-transfer example with units carried through

Derive Coulomb's law experimentally and mathematically: present experimental evidence for inverse-square dependence, then derive vector form F = k q1 q2 r̂ / r² showing units (N) step by step and anchoring to a concrete example (two 1.0 μC charges separated by 0.10 m)

Demonstration/measurement: teacher demo or video of a torsion-balance style set-up (or simulation) measuring force vs distance, students extract numerical values and check units (N) and proportionality to q1q2/r²

Guided practice: pairs solve two worked problems — (a) compute magnitude and direction of force between specified q1, q2, r with units; (b) compute net force from three charges using superposition (students write vector sum steps and units)

Check and consolidate: short 5-minute quiz of 2 items (one calculation, one conceptual on quantisation/conservation) followed by whole-class review of answers and statement of how this enables 'Electric field, Test charge and source charge'

periods.title: Charge Quantisation and Coulomb's Law

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds directly on 'Charge Quantisation and Coulomb's Law' by reinterpreting Coulomb force as a field surrounding a source charge; it prepares students to apply the 'Superposition principle for electric field' and to compute flux and dipole behaviour in the next period.

time_allocation.label: Activate prior knowledge: quick review of Coulomb's law and charge sign (talk and 2 quick questions), recalling units (N, C) and inverse-square behaviour
Introduce electric field concept: derive E = F/q_test from Coulomb's law step-by-step using a point charge Q and a +1.0 μC test charge at distance r (show units N/C and N·m/C where they arise)

Demonstration / measurement: instructor-led desk demo using two charged spheres and a small test probe (qualitative needle deflection or force sensor), record measured force (N) and compute E (N/C) at measured r (m)
Guided practice: pairs solve two worked examples—compute magnitude and direction of E for Q = +5.0 μC and Q = −3.0 μC at given r values (carry units N/C and show r̂ direction explicitly)

Check and consolidate: short formative quiz (3 items) including one conceptual question about test vs source charge and one numerical with unit check, then instructor summarises main definitions and units

periods.title: Defining and Calculating Electric Field

periods.sequence_rationale: Builds directly on 'Defining and Calculating Electric Field' by using the superposition idea and field vectors to combine point-charge fields into a dipole description; it makes possible calculating the dipole's torque in a uniform field and prepares students for 'Dipole field far-field behaviour, Gauss's law, Coulomb's law'.

time_allocation.label: Activate prior knowledge: quick review of electric field vectors and superposition with one worked example using two point charges (show units N/C and m explicitly)

Introduce new material: define electric dipole and dipole moment p = q·2a (derive p magnitude and direction from two point charges, carry units C·m), and define electric flux E·dS with units (N/C)·m^2
Demonstration: classroom apparatus or diagram of a dipole in a uniform electric field; show vector forces on charges, measure/compute resulting torque step-by-step to obtain τ = p × E with units N·m

Guided practice: pairs work through two problems — (a) compute p for given q and separation (include units), (b) compute torque magnitude and direction for a dipole at an angle in a uniform E, deriving τ = pE sinθ
Check for understanding: 3 short conceptual questions (does net force occur? why net charge zero gives no net force in uniform E; compute numerical torque) with quick individual answers and units
Consolidate and bridge: teacher summarises results, emphasizes derivations and units, and explains how this leads into analysing dipole far-field behaviour and using Gauss's law/Coulomb's law next

periods.title: Electric Dipole, Dipole Moment and Torque

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds on the prior 'Electric Dipole, Dipole Moment and Torque' ideas of superposition, electric flux and the dipole moment p to derive the dipole's far-field 1/r^3 behaviour and to compute torque τ = p × E with units. It prepares students to apply Gauss's law and far-field approximations when moving to continuous charge densities and the fields of wires, planes and spherical shells in the next period.

time_allocation.label: Activate prior knowledge: brief recall of dipole moment p (C·m), superposition and Coulomb's law with units (N·m^2/C^2 or k), and electric flux definition (V·m or N·m^2/C) — quick warm-up example

Introduce new derivations: step-by-step derivation of dipole far-field E ∝ 1/r^3 using two opposite point charges separated by 2a, carrying units through each step (m, C, N); explicit statement of axis vs equatorial sign

Demonstration and measurement: teacher demo with two small charged spheres on a jig (charges ±q, separation 2a) showing torque in a uniform external field and qualitative falloff of field with distance; students note measured quantities and units

Guided problem set: pairs compute torque τ = p × E (units N·m) for given p and E, and calculate numerical dipole-field values at r≫a using p (C·m) and ε0; teacher circulates and derives any algebraic steps requested

Formative check: short written quiz (2 problems) — (1) state whether net force on ideal dipole in uniform E is zero and explain units, (2) compute ratio of dipole field at two distances; immediate marking and quick feedback
Consolidation and homework: summarise key derivations (show final formula with units), assign problems linking dipole far-field approximations to upcoming Gauss's-law applications

periods.title: Dipole Far‑Field, Torque and Gauss's Law

periods.sequence_rationale: Builds on Dipole Far‑Field, Torque and Gauss's Law by applying Gauss's law and Coulomb's law to continuous charge distributions; completes the module by deriving concrete field formulas for infinite plane, infinite wire, and thin spherical shell which students can use for problem solving and comparisons to point‑charge results.

time_allocation.label: Activate prior knowledge: quick review of Gauss's law statement and units (flux = Q_enclosed/ε0), relate to Coulomb's law with a point charge example (carry units C, m, N/C)
Derive field of infinite plane: set up Gaussian pillbox, show dQ = σ dA (σ in C/m^2), compute flux and solve E = σ/(2ε0), point to a physical example (charged metal plate) and state units N/C
Derive field of infinite wire: choose cylindrical Gaussian surface, express dQ = λ dl (λ in C/m), compute flux and solve E = λ/(2π ε0 r), anchor with a charged thin wire example and carry units N/C

Derive field of thin spherical shell: use spherical Gaussian surface, show Q = ∫ρ dV reduces to total q for shell (q in C), derive E = q/(4π ε0 r^2) outside and E=0 inside, compare to point charge and state units N/C

Guided practice: teacher-led problem set (pairs) — (a) compute E at 2 cm from λ=5 nC/m wire, (b) E near a σ=10 μC/m^2 plane at 1 mm, (c) E inside/outside shell with q=2 μC at specified r; require showing units at each step

Check and consolidate: quick formative quiz (3 short calculations and one conceptual question about superposition), discuss common errors and physical interpretation (direction, dependence on r), summarize takeaways

unsupported_claims.claim: Superposition principle for electric field: The total electric field at a point due to a system of point charges is the vector sum of fields produced by individual charges.
Gauss's law: The total electric flux through any closed surface equals the total charge enclosed divided by epsilon_0.

Continuous charge densities (linear, surface, volume): Definitions of macroscopic charge densities: surface density sigma = dQ/dA, linear density lambda = dQ/dl, volume density rho = dQ/dV with SI units C/m^2, C/m, C/m^3 respectively.
Electric field of a point charge (element) E = (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) (q / r^2) r̂
Superposition sum for fields E(r) = sum_i [ (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) (q_i / r_{iP}^2) r̂_{iP} ]
Far-field dipole equatorial formula E (on equatorial plane, r>>a) = - (1/(4 pi epsilon_0)) (p / r^3)
Gauss's law (integral) Flux through closed surface = enclosed charge / epsilon_0
Field of uniformly charged spherical shell (outside/inside) Outside: E = q/(4 pi epsilon_0 r^2); Inside: E = 0 (for r<R)
Rubbing two objects creates new electric charge — when I rub a rod on fur (or two materials together) I make charge out of nothing so the total amount of charge in the system increases.
